title: From flower to fruit: the parts of a flower, pollination, and how each seed begins with one pollen grain

summary.text: The pollen of a hibiscus flower lands on the stigma, at the very top of the flower. The ovules, which become the seeds, are about 7 centimetres below, sealed inside the ovary. So how does pollen on the outside start a seed on the inside? Your child takes a flower apart and names the four rings of parts: sepals, petals, stamens and carpels. They learn that pollination only brings the pollen to the stigma. After that, each pollen grain grows a thin tube down to one ovule. A male cell joins the egg cell there. That joining is fertilisation. Then the ovary grows into the fruit, and each fertilised ovule grows into a seed. In the Empty Places Test, your child opens 20 pods and counts the seeds and the ovules that never grew.
summary.art: A red hibiscus flower cut in half from top to bottom, with a dotted line running from a pollen grain on a stigma at the top down to a small ovule in the ovary at the bottom, beside an open pea pod with five peas and two tiny empty places.

intro.hook: Open a pea pod and count. You may find five fat peas, and two tiny pale specks that never grew. All seven sat in the same pod, on the same plant, with the same water and light. Why did five become seeds and two did not?
intro.text: The answer starts in the flower, weeks before the pod was picked. In this unit you first take a hibiscus flower apart, ring by ring. You find the parts that make pollen and the part that holds the ovules. You learn how pollen travels from flower to flower, and what happens after the pollen lands. Then you open 20 pods and count the seeds and the empty places. You also drop a rain of moong seeds to see how much pollen the wind wastes. By the end you can say what each seed needed before that seed could begin.
intro.art: A child's hands holding an open pea pod over a steel plate, with five round peas and two tiny pale specks still attached along the seam of the pod.

outcomes: I can find the four rings of a real flower, and name the parts of a stamen and a carpel.
I can say what job each part of a flower does.
I can explain what pollination is, and tell self-pollination from cross-pollination.
I can tell from a flower's features whether the wind or an animal probably carries the pollen.
I can explain fertilisation: a pollen tube carries a male cell to the egg cell inside an ovule.
I can say which part of a flower grows into the fruit, and which part grows into each seed.
I can explain why a fruit can have empty places: each seed needs their own pollen grain.
I can count results from many pods or many runs, and say why one count is not enough.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that makes seeds. A complete flower has four rings of parts: sepals, petals, stamens and carpels.
terms.example: A hibiscus flower has 5 sepals, 5 petals, many stamens and 5 joined carpels.
terms.art: A hibiscus flower seen from the side, with the four rings of parts marked by four curved lines.

terms.meaning: One of the small leaf-like parts in the outer ring of a flower. The sepals cover and protect the bud before the flower opens.
terms.example: The green cap on top of a brinjal or a tomato is made of the flower's sepals.
terms.art: A closed green flower bud with the sepals wrapped round it, beside a tomato with a green star of sepals on top.

terms.meaning: One of the parts in the second ring of a flower. Petals are often brightly coloured or scented, and they help animal visitors find the flower.
terms.example: A hibiscus has 5 large red petals. A paddy flower has none.
terms.art: Five red petals laid out in a fan on white paper.

terms.meaning: The male part of a flower. A stamen is a thin stalk called a filament, with an anther on top that makes pollen.
terms.example: A mustard flower has 6 stamens. A hibiscus has more than 50.
terms.art: One stamen drawn large: a thin stalk with a yellow two-lobed head.

terms.meaning: The head of a stamen. The anther makes pollen grains, and splits open to let them out when they are ripe.
terms.example: Touch the yellow anthers of a hibiscus, and yellow pollen comes off on your finger.
terms.art: A yellow anther split open along a line, with pollen grains spilling out.

terms.meaning: The stalk of a stamen. The filament holds the anther up where a visitor or the wind can reach the pollen.
terms.example: The anthers of a paddy flower hang outside the flower on long, thin filaments.
terms.art: A grass flower with three anthers dangling on thread-like stalks.

terms.meaning: A tiny living grain made in an anther. Each pollen grain carries the male cells that can fertilise an ovule.
terms.example: A maize pollen grain is about one tenth of a millimetre wide, like a speck of yellow dust.
terms.art: A fingertip dusted with yellow powder, and a circle showing a few of the grains drawn large, round and spiky.

terms.meaning: The female part of a flower. A carpel has a stigma on top, a style in the middle and an ovary at the bottom. Many flowers have several carpels joined into one. The female part is also called the pistil.
terms.example: A pea flower has 1 carpel, which becomes the pod. A hibiscus has 5 carpels joined together.
terms.art: A single carpel drawn large, shaped like a long-necked bottle, with stigma, style and ovary labelled.

terms.meaning: The top of a carpel. The stigma is sticky or feathery, and catches pollen grains.
terms.example: A hibiscus has 5 round, velvety stigmas at the very tip of the flower.
terms.art: Five small round red pads at the end of a long column, with yellow grains stuck to them.

terms.meaning: The stalk of a carpel. The style joins the stigma to the ovary, and pollen tubes grow down through it.
terms.example: Each silk thread on a maize cob is one very long style.
terms.art: A thin stalk joining a round stigma at the top to a swollen ovary at the bottom.

terms.meaning: The swollen base of a carpel. The ovary holds the ovules, and grows into the fruit after fertilisation.
terms.example: The small green swelling at the base of a bhindi flower is the ovary. It grows into the bhindi.
terms.art: A flower with the petals removed, showing a small green swelling at the base, and beside it the same swelling grown into a pod.

terms.meaning: A tiny grain inside the ovary that holds one egg cell. A fertilised ovule grows into a seed.
terms.example: A pea flower's ovary holds about 6 to 10 ovules in a row. Each can become one pea.
terms.art: An ovary cut open to show a row of tiny pale grains on short stalks.

terms.meaning: A sugary liquid that many flowers make. Animals visit flowers to drink nectar, and they carry pollen away on their bodies.
terms.example: Pull out an ixora flower and you find a drop of sweet nectar at the base of the thin tube.
terms.art: A drop of clear liquid at the bottom of a flower tube, with a butterfly's long tongue reaching down to the drop.

terms.meaning: The carrying of pollen from an anther to a stigma of the same kind of plant. The wind, water or an animal carries the pollen.
terms.example: A bee who visits one pumpkin flower and then another carries pollen from anther to stigma.
terms.art: A bee with yellow dust on her hairs flying from one yellow flower to another.

terms.meaning: Pollination in which the pollen comes from the same flower, or from another flower on the same plant.
terms.example: A pea flower pollinates itself inside the closed bud, before the flower opens.
terms.art: One flower with a short arrow from its own anther to its own stigma.

terms.meaning: Pollination in which the pollen comes from a different plant of the same kind.
terms.example: A female papaya tree can make fruit with seeds only if pollen comes from another papaya tree.
terms.art: Two plants of the same kind with a long arrow from the anther of one to the stigma of the other.

terms.meaning: An animal who carries pollen from flower to flower. Bees, flies, butterflies, moths, beetles, birds and bats are pollinators.
terms.example: Sunbirds pollinate the red flowers of the silk cotton tree. Moths pollinate the white tuberose at night.
terms.art: A sunbird with a curved beak drinking from a large red flower, with pollen dusted on her forehead.

terms.meaning: A very thin tube that a pollen grain grows after landing on a stigma. The tube grows down the style to an ovule and carries the male cells there.
terms.example: In maize, a pollen tube grows down a silk that can be 20 centimetres long, in about one day.
terms.art: A cut-open carpel with a pollen grain on the stigma and a thin tube running from the grain down to one ovule.

terms.meaning: The joining of a male cell from a pollen grain with the egg cell inside an ovule. A seed begins only after fertilisation.
terms.example: Pollination puts pollen on a bhindi's stigma. Fertilisation happens later, deep inside the ovary.
terms.art: An ovule drawn large, with the tip of a pollen tube touching it and two small cells about to join.

terms.meaning: The young plant inside a seed. The embryo grows from the fertilised egg cell.
terms.example: Split a soaked chana and you find the embryo as a tiny root and shoot between the two halves.
terms.art: A split chana seed with a tiny curved root and shoot at one end.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that grows from the ovary of a flower and holds the seeds.
terms.example: A mango, a bhindi, a pea pod, a tomato and a grain of paddy are all fruits.
terms.art: A mango, a bhindi, a pea pod and a tomato in a row, each cut open to show the seeds.

explanations.concept: The four rings of a flower
explanations.definition: A complete flower has four rings of parts, one inside the other. From the outside in, they are the sepals, the petals, the stamens and the carpels.
explanations.description: Look at a flower from the outside in. The outer ring is the sepals. They are usually green, and they cover the bud before the flower opens. The second ring is the petals. Petals are often large and coloured, and many have a scent. They help animal visitors find the flower. The third ring is the stamens, which are the male parts. Each stamen makes pollen. In the middle are the carpels, which are the female part. The carpels hold the ovules, and the ovules can become seeds. The number of parts in each ring is often the same, or one number is a multiple of the other. A hibiscus has 5 sepals, 5 petals and 5 carpels. A mustard flower has 4 sepals, 4 petals and 6 stamens. Not every flower has all four rings. A paddy flower has no petals. A pumpkin vine makes some flowers with only stamens and other flowers with only carpels.
examples: Hibiscus: 5 sepals, 5 petals, more than 50 stamens joined in a tube, and 5 carpels joined together.
Mustard: 4 sepals, 4 yellow petals in a cross, 6 stamens and 1 long, thin ovary.
Tuberose (rajnigandha or sampangi): 6 white petal-like parts, 6 stamens and 3 joined carpels.
explanations.art: A flower drawn from above as four rings, one inside the other, coloured green, red, yellow and pale green, and labelled sepals, petals, stamens and carpels.

explanations.concept: The stamen: where pollen is made
explanations.definition: A stamen is the male part of a flower. A stamen has a stalk called the filament, and a head called the anther. The anther makes the pollen grains.
explanations.description: The anther is a small bag with two halves. Inside, thousands of pollen grains form. When the pollen is ripe, the anther dries and splits open. The filament holds the anther in the right place. In a hibiscus, the filaments are joined into a long tube. The anthers stand out from the tube like small yellow buttons. In a grass flower, the filaments are long and thin, so the anthers hang out and shake in the wind. A pollen grain is alive. Each grain has a tough outer wall, and carries male cells inside. Pollen grains are very small. A maize pollen grain is about one tenth of a millimetre wide, and most pollen grains are smaller. Each kind of plant has pollen with a different shape and pattern. Under a microscope, a scientist can name a plant from one pollen grain. The wall is so tough that pollen grains in old mud can last for thousands of years.
examples: One maize tassel sheds millions of pollen grains in about a week.
Pumpkin pollen grains are large, sticky and spiky, and they cling to the hairs of a bee.
Scientists read pollen grains in old lake mud to find out which plants grew there long ago.
explanations.art: A stamen drawn large with filament and anther labelled, and a circle showing three different pollen grains under a microscope: one smooth and round, one spiky, one with a net pattern.

explanations.concept: The carpel: stigma, style, ovary and ovules
explanations.definition: A carpel is the female part of a flower. The stigma catches pollen, the style joins the stigma to the ovary, and the ovary holds the ovules.
explanations.description: The stigma is at the top, where pollen can reach it. A stigma is sticky, velvety or feathery, so pollen grains stay on. The style is a stalk that holds the stigma up. At the bottom is the ovary, a closed chamber. Inside the ovary are the ovules. An ovule is a tiny grain on a short stalk, and each ovule holds one egg cell. A pea flower has one carpel with about 6 to 10 ovules in a row. In many flowers, several carpels are joined side by side into one female part. Then you can often count them. A hibiscus has 5 stigmas at the tip, and the ovary has 5 chambers. So the female part of a hibiscus is 5 carpels joined together. The chambers stay when the ovary grows into a fruit. That is why a bhindi, cut across, shows 5 chambers or more, and a cucumber shows 3. The ovules are sealed inside the ovary. Nothing from outside touches them, except a pollen tube.
examples: Pea, bean and groundnut flowers have 1 carpel. The pod is that one carpel grown big.
Bhindi belongs to the hibiscus family. A bhindi cut across usually shows 5 chambers.
Each segment of an orange grew from one carpel of the orange flower.
explanations.art: A carpel drawn large with stigma, style and ovary labelled, and the ovary cut open to show ovules, beside a bhindi cut across to show five chambers.

explanations.concept: Pollination: how pollen reaches a stigma
explanations.definition: Pollination is the carrying of pollen from an anther to a stigma of the same kind of plant. In self-pollination the pollen comes from the same plant. In cross-pollination the pollen comes from a different plant.
explanations.description: A plant cannot walk to another plant, so something must carry the pollen. In most kinds of flowering plants, an animal carries the pollen. Nearly 9 out of 10 kinds are pollinated by animals: bees, flies, beetles, butterflies, moths, birds and bats. The animal comes for food, which is nectar or the pollen itself. Pollen sticks to the animal's body and rubs off on the stigma of the next flower. In other plants, the wind carries the pollen. Paddy, wheat, maize, ragi, bamboo and all the grasses are wind-pollinated. A few water plants let pollen float on the water. Some plants pollinate themselves. A pea flower sheds pollen on its own stigma inside the closed bud. Self-pollination is sure, because no carrier is needed. Cross-pollination mixes two different parents, so the young plants differ more from each other. Some of them may then live through a disease or a dry year that kills the others.
examples: Mango flowers are pollinated mostly by flies and small bees.
Tape grass, a pond plant, lets the male flowers float across the water to the female flowers.
Pea, groundnut, paddy, wheat and tomato plants mostly pollinate themselves.
explanations.art: Three small scenes side by side: a bee carrying pollen between two flowers, wind blowing a cloud of pollen from a maize tassel, and a closed pea bud with an arrow from its own anther to its own stigma.

explanations.concept: Wind flowers and visitor flowers look different
explanations.definition: A flower pollinated by animals has features that bring visitors and put pollen on them. A flower pollinated by wind has features that release pollen into the air and catch it from the air.
explanations.description: You can often tell how a flower is pollinated by looking. A flower pollinated by insects usually has bright or white petals, a scent and nectar. The pollen is sticky or spiky, and there is not very much of it. The stigma is sticky and sits where the visitor's body will touch it. A flower pollinated by birds is often red or orange, with a lot of thin nectar and little scent. A flower pollinated by moths or bats is often white or pale. It opens in the evening and smells strongest at night. A flower pollinated by wind has no need of visitors. The petals are tiny or missing, and there is no scent and no nectar. The anthers hang out of the flower on long filaments. The pollen is dry, smooth and light, and there is a huge amount of it. The stigmas are long and feathery, and they stand out in the moving air. Colour, scent and nectar all cost the plant food. A wind flower spends that food on extra pollen.
examples: Paddy: no petals, anthers hanging out, feathery stigmas. Wind.
Red silk cotton tree: large red cups full of nectar, little scent. Birds such as mynas and sunbirds.
Tuberose: white, opens in the evening, strong scent at night. Moths.
explanations.art: A split picture: on one side a bright flower with a bee, a sticky stigma and a few spiky pollen grains, on the other a green grass flower with dangling anthers, feathery stigmas and a cloud of smooth pollen.

explanations.concept: Fertilisation: the pollen tube and the joining of two cells
explanations.definition: Fertilisation is the joining of a male cell from a pollen grain with the egg cell inside an ovule. A pollen tube carries the male cell from the stigma to the ovule.
explanations.description: Pollination ends when a pollen grain lands on a stigma. The grain is still on the outside of the carpel. The egg cell is inside an ovule, deep in the ovary. The pollen grain takes in water and sugar from the stigma. Then the grain grows a tube, much thinner than a hair. The tube pushes down between the cells of the style and into the ovary. The tip of the tube enters one ovule through a tiny opening. The tube carries two male cells. One male cell joins the egg cell, and this joining is fertilisation. The fertilised egg cell now has instructions from two parents. This cell divides again and again and grows into the embryo, the young plant in the seed. The second male cell joins another cell in the ovule. In rice, wheat, maize and coconut, that second joining grows into the seed's food store. One pollen tube fertilises one ovule. A flower with 8 ovules needs at least 8 pollen grains to fill every place.
examples: In maize, a pollen tube grows down a silk up to 30 centimetres long, in about one day.
The white part of a grain of rice and the white flesh of a coconut grew from the second joining.
In peas and beans, the young plant takes in that food store early. The food is then kept in two thick seed leaves.
explanations.art: A carpel cut open from top to bottom: three pollen grains on the stigma, three thin tubes growing down the style, and each tube ending at a different ovule in the ovary.

explanations.concept: From flower to fruit: what each part becomes
explanations.definition: After fertilisation, the ovary grows into the fruit and each fertilised ovule grows into a seed. The petals and stamens have finished their work, and they dry up and fall.
explanations.description: A fruit is a grown ovary. A seed is a grown ovule. The wall of the ovary becomes the wall of the fruit: the skin and flesh of a mango, the green case of a pea pod, the shell of a groundnut. The coat of the ovule becomes the seed coat. Inside, the fertilised egg cell becomes the embryo. The other parts of the flower leave signs that you can find. The petals and stamens usually fall within a few days. The sepals often stay on. They are the green cap of a brinjal and the green star on a tomato. The dry tip at the far end of a pea pod is what is left of the style and stigma. The brown threads at the end of a maize cob are dried styles. To a botanist, anything that grew from an ovary and holds seeds is a fruit. So a tomato, a bhindi, a cucumber, a chilli, a pea pod and a grain of paddy are all fruits.
examples: Bhindi: the yellow flower lasts one day. The ovary left behind grows into a pod about 10 centimetres long in a week.
Mango: thousands of tiny flowers open on one branch, and only a few ovaries grow into mangoes.
Pea: the pod is the ovary wall, and each pea is one ovule grown into a seed.
explanations.art: Four drawings of a pea flower in a row: the open flower, the flower with petals falling and a tiny green pod showing, a half-grown pod, and a full pod with the dry style at the tip and sepals at the stalk.

explanations.concept: One pollen grain for each seed: why fruits have empty places
explanations.definition: Each ovule is fertilised separately, by one pollen tube from one pollen grain. An ovule that is not fertilised does not grow into a seed. That ovule stays as a tiny empty place in the fruit.
explanations.description: A maize cob shows this rule most clearly. A young cob has about 500 ovules in rows. Each ovule has a style of their own, which is one silk thread. The silks grow out past the tip of the husk and catch pollen from the wind. Where a silk gets a pollen grain, a kernel grows. Where a silk gets none, that place on the cob stays bare. The same thing happens inside a pea pod, though you cannot see the styles. An ovule that no pollen tube reached stays tiny and pale. Sometimes an ovule is fertilised and still stops growing, because the plant does not send that seed enough food. By looking, you cannot always tell which of the two happened. The young seeds also tell the fruit to grow. In 1950, the scientist Jean Nitsch picked the tiny seed-like fruits off one side of young strawberries. The red flesh on that side stopped growing. So a fruit often grows lopsided, or pinched, where seeds are missing.
examples: An apple has 5 carpels and up to 10 seeds. An apple with seeds on only one side often grows lopsided.
A long bean pod is thin and pinched at a place where a seed did not grow.
A maize cob is often bare at the tip, because the silks from the tip come out last.
explanations.art: A maize cob with full rows at the bottom and bare patches near the tip, with silk threads drawn from several kernels and from several bare dots, and one silk shown with a pollen grain on its end.

explanations.concept: How flowers keep out their own pollen, and why some do not
explanations.definition: Many plants have features that stop a flower's own pollen from fertilising the ovules. Then every seed has two different parents. Other plants pollinate themselves, which is sure but mixes nothing new.
explanations.description: A flower with stamens and carpels close together could easily pollinate itself. Many plants prevent this. Some keep the two apart in space. In a hibiscus, the stigmas stand beyond the anthers, at the very tip. A pumpkin vine makes male flowers and female flowers. Papaya and date palm go further: some trees make only male flowers, and others only female flowers. Some plants keep the two apart in time. In a custard apple flower, the stigmas are ready first. The anthers shed pollen only later, when the stigmas of that flower have dried. In many other plants, the stigma tests the pollen. The stigma of a cabbage or radish flower recognises pollen from the same plant, and that pollen grows no tube. The plant senses whose pollen has arrived, and decides which grains may grow. Some scientists call this an automatic response. Self-pollinating plants, such as pea and groundnut, take the other way. They are sure of seeds even when no visitor comes.
examples: Farmers pollinate custard apple and date palm flowers by hand, to be sure of fruit.
A single cabbage plant flowering alone sets almost no seed, though the flowers are full of pollen.
A groundnut flower pollinates itself. Then a stalk grows down and pushes the young ovary into the soil.
explanations.art: Four small drawings: a hibiscus with stigmas beyond the anthers, a pumpkin vine with a male and a female flower, a male and a female papaya tree, and a stigma with one pollen grain growing a tube and another grain not growing.

explanations.concept: Flowers and fruits that are not what they seem
explanations.definition: Some things we call one flower are many flowers together. Some things we call a fruit grew from more than an ovary, or have no seeds at all.
explanations.description: A marigold or a sunflower looks like one flower. It is a head of many small flowers packed together. Each 'petal' of a marigold is a whole small flower, with an ovary of their own at the base. A sunflower head can hold more than 1,000 small flowers, and each sunflower seed grew from one of them. The flowers of a banyan, a peepal or a cluster fig are hidden. They line the inside of the young fig, and tiny wasps crawl in to pollinate them. Fruits can mislead too. A banana of the kind we eat grows without fertilisation. Cut one across and you see three parts, with tiny dark specks in the middle. The three parts are the three carpels, and the specks are ovules that never grew. Wild bananas are full of hard seeds. In an apple, the part we eat grew mostly from the base of the flower. The ovary is the core. A pineapple and a jackfruit each grew from a whole bunch of flowers joined together.
examples: One marigold from a garland can hold more than 100 small flowers.
The cashew 'apple' is a swollen stalk. The real fruit is the grey nut that hangs under it.
Farmers grow seedless bananas from side shoots, because the fruits hold no seeds to sow.
explanations.art: A marigold pulled apart into many small strap-shaped flowers, each with a thin pale ovary at the base, beside a banana cut across to show three parts and tiny dark specks.

explanations.concept: How a pollen tube finds an ovule
explanations.definition: A pollen tube is guided to an ovule by chemical signals. Two cells beside the egg cell give out small proteins, and the tip of the tube grows towards them.
explanations.description: A pollen tube has a long way to go and no eyes. For more than a hundred years, botanists asked how the tube finds the tiny opening of an ovule. In 2001, Tetsuya Higashiyama and his team in Japan worked with the wishbone flower. The ovules of this flower can be watched under a microscope. Beside each egg cell lie two helper cells. The team destroyed these cells one at a time with a very fine laser beam. When both helper cells were gone, the pollen tubes wandered and did not find the ovule. In 2009, the same group found the signals. They are small proteins, which the scientists named LUREs. Each kind of plant makes a slightly different LURE. So a tube is drawn best to ovules of the same kind of plant. Once one tube has entered an ovule, the signal stops. Then later tubes turn away and look for other ovules. The ovule calls the tube, and the tube senses the call and steers. Some scientists describe this only as chemistry.
examples: A pollen tube of the wishbone flower turns towards an ovule from a short distance away, less than a millimetre.
In maize, the fastest pollen tubes grow about 1 centimetre in an hour.
Pollen from another kind of plant usually grows no tube, or the tube stops in the style.
explanations.art: A microscope view of a pollen tube bending towards the opening of an ovule, with small dots spreading out from two cells beside the egg cell.

explanations.definition: Nectar, scent, colour and pollen are all made from the food that the plant's leaves make with sunlight. A plant pays visitors with part of that food.
explanations.description: A plant's leaves use the energy of sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. Nectar is sugar dissolved in water, and the plant gives the nectar away. A bee drinks the nectar and uses the energy of the sugar to fly. So the energy that carries pollen from flower to flower came from the Sun, through a leaf. Petals, scent and pollen are also built from that sugar, together with minerals from the soil. This is a cost, and plants spend with care. A flower that has been pollinated often stops making nectar and drops the petals within a day. A wind-pollinated plant spends nothing on nectar or petals. The wind is free, but most of the pollen is lost. So the plant spends the food on making far more pollen. The wind itself is also moved by the Sun, which warms some parts of the Earth more than others.
examples: A hibiscus flower lasts one day. Keeping a large petal fresh costs water and food.
Honey is nectar that bees have dried and stored. A spoon of honey is sunlight caught by many leaves.
A paddy flower opens for an hour or two, sheds pollen into the air and closes.
explanations.art: The Sun shining on a leaf, an arrow from the leaf to a drop of nectar in a flower, and an arrow from the nectar to a bee in flight carrying pollen.

explanations.concept: Does a plant choose which pollen fertilises the ovules?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that a stigma can recognise pollen and stop some grains from growing tubes. They disagree about how far a plant goes on choosing among the grains that are allowed.
explanations.description: Often a stigma receives far more pollen grains than the ovary has ovules. The grains may come from several different plants. All their tubes grow down the same style, and only the first few reach an ovule. In some plants, tubes from certain parents win more often than their numbers predict. The plant also decides which young seeds to feed. A mango tree drops most of the small young fruits, and many pods fill only some of their seeds.
examples: Pollen from the same plant is stopped on the stigma of a cabbage or a radish flower.
When pollen from two parent plants is mixed on one stigma, the seeds do not always come half and half.
A plant with too many young fruits drops some of them, often the ones with the fewest seeds.

perspectives.who: Botanists who study choice by the mother plant
perspectives.explanation: The style is not an empty pipe. It feeds some tubes and slows others, so the mother plant affects which pollen wins. She also stops feeding some young seeds and keeps others. A plant chooses among fathers and among her young.

perspectives.who: Botanists who study the race between pollen tubes
perspectives.explanation: The tubes race, and the fastest win. Some pollen grains simply grow faster tubes. The result looks like a choice by the mother plant. The pollen alone could explain the same result. Good tests must tell the two apart, and that is hard.

Proteins on the pollen fit or do not fit proteins on the stigma. A tube grows where the chemistry allows. On this view, a tube that grows where the chemistry allows is like a key that fits a lock. The word 'choose' should be kept for animals with brains.

explanations.art: A stigma covered in pollen grains of two colours, with many tubes racing down one style towards only four ovules.

explanations.concept: Why are the ovules sealed inside a carpel?
explanations.description: Pine trees and their relatives have no carpels. Their ovules lie open on the scales of a cone, and wind-blown pollen lands right beside them. Plants like these lived for more than 150 million years before the first flowers. In a flowering plant, the ovules are shut inside a closed carpel. Pollen must grow a tube to reach them. The oldest fossil flowers found so far are about 130 million years old. Nobody saw how the carpel began, so there are only ideas. One idea is protection. Beetles came to eat pollen and would have eaten open ovules too, so a closed case kept the ovules safe. A second idea is testing. With the ovules sealed in, every pollen grain must pass the stigma and the style. There the plant can stop the wrong ones. A third idea is speed. A pine takes about a year from pollination to fertilisation. A flowering plant often takes a day or two. All three may be partly right.
examples: A pine seed cone holds the ovules on open scales, with no ovary round them.
Some of the oldest known flower fossils come from rocks in Spain and China, about 125 to 130 million years old.
Magnolia flowers, which are of an old kind, are still pollinated by beetles.
explanations.art: A pine cone scale with two open ovules beside a flower carpel cut open to show ovules sealed inside, with a beetle walking on each.

agreed.text: A seed forms only after pollination and then fertilisation. Pollen must reach the stigma, and a male cell must join the egg cell in the ovule.
agreed.evidence: When flowers are covered so that no pollen can reach them, plants that cannot pollinate themselves set no seed. Charles Darwin covered 100 heads of red clover, and they made no seeds at all.

agreed.text: The ovary of the flower grows into the fruit, and the ovules grow into the seeds.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can watch it on a bhindi, a pea or a pumpkin plant. The same swelling at the base of the flower grows, day by day, into the fruit.

agreed.text: Each ovule is fertilised by one pollen tube.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, one tube is seen to enter each ovule. On a maize cob, each kernel has one silk, and a kernel grows only where the silk received pollen.

agreed.text: A pollen tube carries two male cells. One joins the egg cell, and the other starts the food store of the seed.
agreed.evidence: Sergei Nawaschin saw both joinings under the microscope in lilies in 1898. Many scientists have seen them since, in many kinds of plants.

agreed.text: Flowers pollinated by wind and flowers pollinated by animals differ in regular ways: in petals, scent, nectar, pollen and stigmas.
agreed.evidence: Botanists have compared thousands of kinds of flowers with the carriers seen on them. Wind-pollinated grasses all share small dull flowers, hanging anthers and feathery stigmas.

agreed.text: Nearly 9 out of 10 kinds of flowering plants are pollinated by animals.
agreed.evidence: In 2011, scientists put together studies of plant communities from around the world and counted the share pollinated by animals.

challenging.claim: Once a flower is pollinated, a fruit with seeds is sure to grow.
challenging.for: Fruits do follow pollination, and farmers speak of a flower 'setting' once the bees have come.
challenging.against: Pollination only puts pollen on the stigma. Each grain must still grow a tube, and a male cell must join an egg cell. Pollen of the wrong kind, great heat or a dry stigma can stop this.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that pollination and fertilisation are the same event.

challenging.claim: A fruit is something sweet that we eat raw.
challenging.who: The everyday meaning of the word, used in kitchens and markets.
challenging.for: In cooking, the word is useful. It separates mangoes and bananas from brinjals and beans.
challenging.against: To a botanist, a fruit is a grown ovary that holds seeds. A brinjal, a bhindi, a chilli and a pea pod are fruits. Both meanings are in use, and each suits a different job.
challenging.context: This card is about two meanings of the word 'fruit': the cook's meaning and the botanist's meaning.

challenging.claim: Flowers are colourful and scented to please people.
challenging.who: A common belief, and a belief of many writers in the past.
challenging.for: People enjoy flowers, and gardeners have bred roses and marigolds for size, colour and scent.
challenging.against: Wild flowers had colour and scent for more than a hundred million years before there were people. The colours match what bees, birds and moths can see. Many flowers have patterns that only insects can see.
challenging.context: This card is about why flowers have colour and scent.

challenging.claim: The pollen grain holds the whole young plant, and the ovule is only a place for the young plant to grow.
challenging.who: Matthias Schleiden, a famous German botanist, in 1837.
challenging.for: The pollen tube does enter the ovule, and the embryo first appears just where the tube arrives.
challenging.against: Giovanni Battista Amici showed in 1846 that the egg cell is already in the ovule before the tube arrives. The embryo grows from that egg cell after a male cell joins it.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where the young plant in a seed comes from.

challenging.claim: The mother plant chooses which pollen grains become the fathers of her seeds.
challenging.for: Stigmas stop pollen from the same plant. In some plants, pollen from certain parents wins more often than chance predicts. Plants also drop some young fruits and keep others.
challenging.against: The same results could come from some pollen grains simply growing faster tubes. Tests that separate the two are hard to do, and the results differ from plant to plant.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument among botanists: does the mother plant choose among pollen grains?

big_questions.q: A pea pod holds five peas. Is the pod one fruit, or five young plants with a shared case?
big_questions.hint: Think about what grew from the mother plant's ovary, and what began at each fertilisation.

big_questions.q: Every seed has two parents. Why is having two parents worth the trouble of moving pollen?
big_questions.hint: Think about a field where every plant is exactly the same, and a new disease arrives.

big_questions.q: A plant makes the colour of a flower, but the colour fits the eyes of a bee. So whose colour is it?
big_questions.hint: Think about red flowers in a place with no birds, or scented flowers in a place with no insects.

big_questions.q: A stigma lets some pollen grow and stops other pollen. Is that choosing?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you mean when you say that you choose. Then ask which parts of that the stigma does.

big_questions.q: Most of the food on your plate began with a pollen grain landing. Who should look after the carriers of pollen?
big_questions.hint: Think about farmers, city families with balconies, and people who make and sell insect sprays.

big_questions.q: Farmers grow bananas that make no seeds. Is it fair to the plant to grow fruit that can never become new plants by seed?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the banana plant gets from farmers, and what the plant loses.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what pollen does after landing on a stigma? This card tells the true story of Giovanni Battista Amici, who first saw a pollen tube.
how_we_found_out.story: By 1700, botanists knew that a flower makes no seeds without pollen. But the pollen stays on the stigma, and the seeds form far below, inside the ovary. Many thought that the pollen grain burst and sent down a fine vapour. Giovanni Battista Amici of Modena, in Italy, built some of the best microscopes of his time. In 1823 he was looking at the stigma of a purslane flower. He saw a pollen grain put out a thin tube, which grew down into the stigma. By 1830 he had followed such tubes all the way down the style and into the ovules. Then a new argument began. In 1837 the famous botanist Matthias Schleiden wrote that the tip of the pollen tube itself becomes the young plant. If so, the ovule was only a place for the young plant to grow. In 1846 Amici studied orchids, whose ovules are small and clear. He showed that an egg cell is already waiting in the ovule before the tube arrives. The young plant grows from that egg cell, and only after the tube has reached it. Other botanists soon saw the same.
how_we_found_out.who: Giovanni Battista Amici, an Italian microscope maker and scientist (1786 to 1863)
how_we_found_out.when: Amici first saw a pollen tube in 1823. He followed tubes into the ovules by 1830. In 1846 he showed that the egg cell is in the ovule before the tube arrives.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: First, that pollen sends a vapour down to the ovary. Later, that the tip of the pollen tube becomes the young plant, so that the ovule gives nothing. Amici's microscope showed a real tube, and then an egg cell that was in the ovule before the tube came.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in 1820s clothes looking down a brass microscope by a window, with a purslane plant in a pot beside him and a drawing of a pollen grain with a thin tube on the table.

roots.context: In this unit you took a flower apart, and you counted the seeds and the empty places in 20 pods. Here we ask what those counts show about how a new life begins, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Empty Places Test, one pod held full seeds and also tiny ovules that never grew. All of them sat in the same ovary, on the same mother plant. Each seed began only when a pollen tube reached that one ovule. So a fruit holds many young, and each of them was begun separately.
deep_truth.habit: We count a fruit as one thing, and we say that the plant made a fruit. Inside, the seeds were started one at a time, each by a different pollen grain. Some places in the same fruit were never started at all.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Empty Places Test, you counted the seeds and the empty places in 20 pods. Most pods have at least one ovule that stayed tiny, beside seeds that grew full. On a maize cob, each kernel has one silk, and a kernel grows only where that silk received pollen. If all your own pods were full, write that down, and look at the tip of a maize cob.

three.who_am_i: You also began when two cells joined, one from each parent. Like each pea in a pod, you were begun separately, and nobody else has quite your mix.
three.what_is_life: In a flowering plant, a new life begins when a male cell and an egg cell meet. The plant makes many chances for that meeting, and only some of them happen.
three.what_is_this_world: A fruit on your plate is the result of many meetings: a carrier and a flower, a pollen grain and a stigma, a male cell and an egg cell.

roots.thread: A flower has four rings of parts, and two of the rings make the cells that must meet. The plant cannot bring those cells together alone. The wind, a bee or a bird carries the pollen. Then the pollen grain grows a tube the rest of the way. Each seed is two parents joined into one new plant. Many sages taught that every being arises from a meeting of others, and that all come from one source.

teachings.teaching: Laozi says that the Tao gives birth to One, and One gives birth to Two. Two gives birth to Three, and Three gives birth to all things.
teachings.link: In fertilisation, two cells from two parents join and make a third being, a new plant. All the cells of a banyan tree come from that one cell. Laozi was writing about the whole world, long before anyone saw a pollen tube. The verse and the science share a pattern, and the science does not prove the verse.

teachings.source: The Jain teaching of anekantavada, many-sidedness, with the old story of the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Each blind man touches one part of the elephant and describes the whole animal by that part. Each is right about what he touched. Jain teachers say that truth has many sides, and one view sees only one of them.
teachings.link: A cook sees a pea pod as one vegetable. A botanist sees one ovary grown big. Your count shows several young, each begun separately, and some places never begun. All three are true of the same pod.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: The sutra describes a net with a jewel at every knot. Each jewel reflects every other jewel, so none can be seen apart from the rest.
teachings.link: A flower's colour fits the eyes of the flower's visitors, and a sunbird's beak fits the flowers she drinks from. Each was shaped over a very long time by the other. This is what science has found. The sutra says the same of all things, which science has not tested.

science.text: Each ovule is fertilised by a separate pollen tube, so the seeds in one fruit are begun separately.
When pollen from several plants lands on one stigma, the seeds in one fruit can have different fathers.
Whether the mother plant chooses among the pollen grains, or the fastest tubes simply win, is still argued.

other_view.who: Many botanists who study how fruits grow
other_view.view: The mother plant builds the ovary, feeds every seed, and often stops feeding some of them. Without her, no seed grows at all. On this view a fruit is one piece of the mother plant's work. The seeds become separate beings only when they leave her.

practice.title: One pod, slowly
practice.say: Hold a closed pod flat on your palm. A bhindi will also do. Close your eyes and run one finger slowly along the pod. Feel each bump. Each bump is one seed, and each seed began with one pollen grain. Take one slow breath for each bump. Then open your eyes and open the pod. Count the seeds, and look for a place where no seed grew.
practice.kid: Hold a closed pod on your palm. Close your eyes. Run a finger slowly along the pod. Take one slow breath for each bump. Each bump began with one pollen grain. Now open the pod and look.

ask: A pod has five peas and two empty places. Were there seven beginnings in that pod, or five?
You also began when two cells joined. What can a new being get from two parents that one parent alone cannot give?
The pea plant fed some of the young seeds and stopped feeding others. Does the pod belong to the mother plant, or to the seeds?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed, one finger resting on a green pea pod that lies on the other palm.

story.title: One Thread Each
story.note: Kavana, Ajji, Rudrappa and Sudha Atte are made up, and so are their fields. These things are real. Davanagere district in Karnataka grows a great deal of maize, sown with the June rains. A maize plant has the male flowers in the tassel at the top and the female flowers on the cob below. Each silk thread is the style of one ovule, and a kernel grows only if that silk receives a pollen grain. The wind carries maize pollen. So maize planted in one thin line is often poorly filled, and maize planted in a block fills well. Growers do pollinate small plots by hand, by shaking tassels over the silks.
text: Kavana's grandmother grew maize outside Honnali, on two acres of black soil, and she sowed her field the way she had always sown it. The whole field was one great square, row behind row, so close that the leaves of one plant lay on the shoulders of the next.
That June, Ajji counted sixty seeds into Kavana's hand.
"These are yours," she said. "Sow them where you like. What they give, you sell."

Kavana had thought about it for a long time. She had seen that the plants in the middle of Ajji's square stood in each other's shade. The plants at the edge had sun on one whole side, and they were always the thickest. So she did not plant a square. She sowed all sixty seeds in a single line along the bund beside the road, where every plant would have sun on both sides and nobody's leaves on a neighbour.

It worked. By August her line was the tallest maize in the village. People slowed their cycles to look at it. At the top of each plant a tassel opened like a small brown broom, and in the mornings, when the wind came across the bund, yellow dust smoked off the tassels and blew away over the road. Kavana liked to watch it go.
Lower down, each plant put out a cob wrapped in green leaves. From the tip of each cob hung a tuft of pale threads, wet and shining, as fine as hair.
In October they picked. Ajji's cobs came first. Kavana pulled the leaves off one, and the kernels sat in tight rows from the bottom to the very tip, like a mouth with every tooth.
Then she opened the first cob from her own line.
There was a ring of kernels at the bottom. Above that there were a few here and a few there. The rest was bare white cob.
She opened ten more. The best of them was half full.
Everybody had a reason. Rudrappa from the next field said the bund was too dry, so near the road. Sudha Atte said the soil of a bund is always poor. Kavana's cousin said that birds had been at them.
Kavana listened to each of them, and then she went and looked.

A thirsty plant does not grow taller than a watered one, and hers were the tallest. A hungry plant is pale, and hers were dark green to the last leaf. And nothing had eaten her cobs. The leaves around them were whole. The bare places were not chewed. They were smooth, and when she held the cob close she could see that they were not empty either. They were covered with rows of tiny flat white dots, each one sitting exactly where a kernel should have been.
So the places had been there. They had just never grown.

She sat down on the step with one of Ajji's cobs and one of her own, both still in their leaves, and this time she took the leaves off slowly, one at a time. Under the last leaf, the dried brown threads lay flat along the cob, hundreds of them, all running the same way.

She took hold of one thread near the tip and followed it down with her fingernail. It ran between two rows of kernels and ended at a kernel. She tried another. It ended at a different kernel. She tried six more on Ajji's cob. Every thread went to one kernel, and no kernel had two.
Then she did the same on her own cob, over a bare patch. The threads were there too. Each one ended at a flat white dot.
Every place had a thread, then, whether it had grown or not. And every thread ran all the way up and out of the top, into the open air.
"What were you waiting for out there?" she said to the cob.
And she remembered the yellow dust.
She ran to the field. "Ajji! When the dust blows off the tops, where does it land?"
"On everything," said Ajji. "On my head. In August you cannot walk through the middle of the field without turning yellow."

"In the middle of your field. Not on my bund. On my bund the wind crosses the line in one step and takes the dust over the road." Kavana held up the two cobs. "Each thread goes to one grain. I think each thread has to catch a speck of the dust before its grain will grow. Your threads stood in a yellow cloud. Mine caught what they could."

Ajji turned the bare cob over in her hands. "My mother used to say that maize must stand shoulder to shoulder, or the cobs come up toothless," she said. "She never told me why. I do not think she knew."
"I can show you why," said Kavana.
At the far end of her line stood twelve plants she had sown three weeks late, after squirrels dug up the first seeds. Their tassels had only just opened, and their threads were fresh and pale.

She tied a red rag to six of them. Every morning for a week, before the wind got up, she bent each of the six tassels over a steel plate and tapped it until the plate was dusted yellow. Then she tipped the plate over the threads of that plant's cob and turned the cob so that the dust fell on every side. The other six plants she left to the wind.
Three weeks later the cobs were fat enough to roast. She carried all twelve to the step, and Ajji came to watch.
The six that had been left to the wind were like the others, a ring at the bottom and bare cob above.
The six with the red rags were full to the tip. All but one, which had a bare stripe down one side.
"That is where my hand missed," said Kavana. "The dust never reached those threads."
Ajji counted the rows on a full cob and the grains in a row, moving her lips. "More than five hundred," she said.
"Five hundred threads," said Kavana. "So five hundred specks of dust have to find them, one each. Next June I am not leaving that to the road."
Next June she drew her plot in the dust with a stick before she sowed it: eight rows of eight, shoulder to shoulder.
"That is sixty-four," said Ajji. "I gave you sixty."
"Then I need four more," said Kavana, and held out her hand.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kavana gives each plant more sun by sowing a single line, and the plants do grow well. But each kernel on a cob has a thread of its own, the silk. A kernel grows only if that thread catches a pollen grain. In a block of maize the pollen falls on the neighbours. In a single line the wind carries the pollen away. Her test with six dusted cobs and six left to the wind shows it.
ask: Kavana's plants were the tallest in the village. Why did tall, healthy plants still give bare cobs?
The bare places on the cob had tiny white dots, and each dot had a thread. What does that tell you about those places?
Why does maize in a square block fill better than maize in one long line?
Kavana dusted six cobs and left six to the wind. Why did she need the six that she left alone?
One dusted cob had a bare stripe down one side. What does that stripe show about how many pollen grains a cob needs?

games.title: Pollen Race: fill every ovule in your pod
games.context: This is a dice game about what happens between pollination and a full pod. Moong seeds are pollen grains. They must land on your stigma, grow down the style step by step, and reach the six ovules in your ovary.

printables.title: A carpel board for each player: draw it on a sheet of paper, from top to bottom
items: STIGMA: a circle at the top, as big as a coin
STYLE, step 1: a box under the stigma
STYLE, step 2: a box under step 1
STYLE, step 3: a box under step 2
OVARY: a large oval at the bottom, with 6 small circles inside for the 6 ovules

printables.title: What the die means: copy these three lines onto the board
items: 1 or 2: A VISITOR COMES. Put 2 pollen grains on your stigma.
3, 4 or 5: THE TUBES GROW. Move every one of your pollen grains one step down.
6: YOUR CHOICE. Take a visitor, or let the tubes grow.

rules: You need one carpel board for each player, one die, and a bowl of about 20 moong seeds for each player. The moong seeds are pollen grains.
Take turns. On your turn, roll the die once.
If you roll 1 or 2, a visitor comes. Put 2 pollen grains on your stigma.
If you roll 3, 4 or 5, the tubes grow. Move every one of your pollen grains one step down: from the stigma to step 1, from step 1 to step 2, and from step 2 to step 3.
A grain that moves down from step 3 enters the ovary. Put that grain on an empty ovule. That ovule is now fertilised, and will become a seed.
One grain fertilises one ovule. If every ovule is already full, a grain that enters the ovary is taken off the board.
If you roll 6, choose: take a visitor, or let the tubes grow.
The first player to fertilise all 6 ovules has a full pod and wins.
Playing alone? Count your turns. A full pod in 12 turns or fewer is a very good game. Play three times and try to beat your own best.

setup.caption: 2. On a 1 or 2, a visitor comes. Put 2 pollen grains on the stigma.

flow.do: 1. Each player draws a carpel board. 2. Copy the three lines that say what the die means. 3. Put a bowl of moong seeds beside each board.
flow.say: This board is one carpel. Point to the stigma, the style and the ovary. Where does the pollen land first? Where are the ovules?
flow.kid: Draw your carpel board. Draw the stigma, three style steps and the ovary. Draw 6 ovules inside the ovary.
flow.parent: The board shows the order that the unit teaches: pollen lands on the stigma, a tube grows down the style, and the tube reaches an ovule in the ovary.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pollen Race. You draw the board and learn what the die means.

flow.do: Play until one player has 3 ovules fertilised. Then stop and ask the question below.
flow.say: Roll the die and do what it says. Watch which comes first for every grain: landing on the stigma, or reaching an ovule.
flow.kid: Roll the die. Do what it says. Keep going until someone has 3 seeds.

ask.q: You rolled 'the tubes grow', but your stigma and style were empty. What happened, and why?
good: Nothing happened.
There was no pollen on my stigma, so no tube could grow.
Pollination has to happen before fertilisation.

flow.parent: A roll of 3, 4 or 5 does nothing when a player has no grains on the board. That is the point to notice: without pollination there is nothing to grow.
flow.context: In this step of Pollen Race you play the first half of the game.

flow.do: 1. Play on until one player fills all 6 ovules. 2. Each player counts the pollen grains they used and the seeds they made. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Finish the game. Then count how many pollen grains landed on your stigma, and how many ovules were fertilised.
flow.kid: Play until a pod is full. Count your pollen grains. Count your seeds.

ask.q: Did every pollen grain that landed on your stigma fertilise an ovule?
good: No. Some were still in the style when the game ended.
No. Some arrived after all the ovules were full.

check.q: A flower's ovary holds 6 ovules. Only 4 pollen grains land on the stigma. What is the largest number of seeds that can form?
check.why: One pollen grain fertilises one ovule, so 4 grains can start 4 seeds at most. Two ovules stay as empty places. Choosing 6 usually means thinking that one grain is enough for the whole flower.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pollen Race. You finish the game and compare pollen grains with seeds.

games.title: Name the Part: three clues, three points
games.context: This is a clue game about the parts of a flower and what each part does. Each card gives three clues, from hard to easy. The sooner you name the part, the more points you score.

printables.title: 16 clue cards: three clues on the front, the answer on the back

items.f: Clue 1: I am in the outer ring. Clue 2: I covered the bud before the flower opened. Clue 3: I am the green cap on a brinjal.
Clue 1: I am in the second ring. Clue 2: A paddy flower has none of me. Clue 3: My colour and scent help visitors find the flower.
Clue 1: I am the whole male part. Clue 2: A mustard flower has six of me. Clue 3: I am a filament with an anther on top.
Clue 1: I am a small bag with two halves. Clue 2: I split open when I am ripe. Clue 3: I make the pollen.
Clue 1: I am a stalk. Clue 2: In grass flowers I am long and thin. Clue 3: I hold the anther up.
Clue 1: I am alive, with a very tough wall. Clue 2: I am about one tenth of a millimetre wide in maize. Clue 3: I carry the male cells.
Clue 1: I am the whole female part. Clue 2: A pea flower has one of me, and a hibiscus has five joined. Clue 3: I am a stigma, a style and an ovary.
Clue 1: I am at the very top of the carpel. Clue 2: In grasses I am feathery. Clue 3: I catch the pollen.
Clue 1: Pollen tubes grow down through me. Clue 2: In maize I am a long silk thread. Clue 3: I join the stigma to the ovary.
Clue 1: I am a closed chamber. Clue 2: I am the swelling at the base of a bhindi flower. Clue 3: I grow into the fruit.
Clue 1: I sit on a short stalk inside the ovary. Clue 2: I hold one egg cell. Clue 3: I can grow into a seed.
Clue 1: I cost the plant sugar. Clue 2: A wind flower does not make me. Clue 3: Bees, birds and moths come to drink me.
Clue 1: I am thinner than a hair. Clue 2: I carry two male cells. Clue 3: I grow from a pollen grain down to an ovule.
Clue 1: I am an event, and you cannot see me happen. Clue 2: I come after pollination. Clue 3: I am the joining of a male cell and an egg cell.
Clue 1: I grow from a fertilised egg cell. Clue 2: I am inside every seed. Clue 3: I am the young plant.
Clue 1: I am a grown ovary. Clue 2: A tomato and a pea pod are both me. Clue 3: I hold the seeds.

rules: You need the 16 clue cards, and paper and a pencil for the scores.
Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the clues facing down.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads clue 1 aloud.
The player on the reader's left may name the part. A right answer after clue 1 scores 3 points.
If the answer is wrong, or the player passes, the reader reads clue 2. A right answer now scores 2 points. After clue 3, a right answer scores 1 point.
Each player gets one guess after each clue. Then the card goes to the bottom of the pile, and the player on the left becomes the reader.
The game ends when every card has been read once. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Cover the card with a sheet of paper. Slide the paper down to show one clue at a time. Say your answer aloud, then turn the card over. Try to score 30 points or more out of 48.

setup.caption: 2. The reader reads clue 1. A right answer now scores 3 points.
