flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Read the rules together. 3. Play one card as practice, with no score.
flow.say: Each card hides one part of a flower, or one event. The first clue is the hardest. Try to name the part before the easy clue.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the rules. Try one card for practice.
flow.context: This is the first step of Name the Part. You make the cards and try one.

flow.do: Play the first 8 cards. Write each player's points. After card 8, ask the question below.
flow.say: Listen to the first clue. Which parts could it be? Guess now, or wait for the next clue.
flow.kid: Listen to clue 1. Guess if you are sure. Wait for the next clue if you are not.

ask.q: Which two parts are the easiest to mix up, and how do you tell them apart?
good: The stigma and the style. The stigma is the top that catches pollen, and the style is the stalk under it.
The ovary and the ovule. The ovary is the chamber, and the ovules are the tiny grains inside.
The anther and the stamen. The anther is only the head of the stamen.

flow.parent: Ovary and ovule are the pair most often mixed up. The ovary becomes the fruit. Each ovule becomes one seed.
flow.context: In this step of Name the Part you play the first eight cards.

flow.do: 1. Play the last 8 cards. 2. Add up the points. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Finish the pile and add up your points. Then answer one last question.
flow.kid: Play the last 8 cards. Add up your points. Answer the question.

check.q: Which part of a flower grows into the fruit?
check.why: The ovary is the chamber that holds the ovules, and the ovary grows into the fruit. Each ovule grows into a seed inside the fruit. Choosing the ovule means the chamber and the grains inside are still mixed up.

flow.context: This is the last step of Name the Part. You finish the cards and check one idea.

experiments.title: The Empty Places Test: does every ovule in a pod become a seed?
experiments.context: In this experiment you open 20 fresh pods from the kitchen. In each pod you count the full seeds, and the tiny ovules that never grew. You find out what share of the ovules became seeds.
experiments.question: Does every ovule in a pod grow into a seed? If not, what share of the ovules became seeds, and where in the pod are the empty places?
experiments.predict: Guess before you open any pod. How many ovules did one pod begin with? Did every one grow into a seed? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Take 20 pods without choosing the fattest ones. Open every pod in the same way, and let the same person decide what counts as a full seed. Count a seed as full when that seed is more than half as big as the biggest seed in the pod. One pod cannot show a pattern, so you count 20 pods and add them up.

materials.item: fresh pods of one kind. Green peas in the pod are best. At other times of year use flat beans (avarai or sem), fresh tuvar pods, double beans or long beans (karamani or chawli)
steel plate
hand lens, or a phone camera that can zoom
notebook and pencil for the results table

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for each pod. Then write these totals: the full seeds, the ovules, and the pods with no empty place. Also add up the empty places at the stalk end, in the middle and at the tip end. Work out the share of ovules that became seeds. Draw a bar chart of how many pods had 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 empty places.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how many of 20 pea pods had 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 empty places
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. In this example the 20 pods held 160 ovules, and 132 of them became seeds. Your own numbers will differ.

setup.art: Twenty green pea pods on a steel plate, with one closed pod held up to show the green cap at the stalk end and the thin dry point at the tip.
setup.caption: 1. Take 20 pods. On one closed pod, find the old sepals and the dry tip of the style.

setup.art: A pea pod opened along the seam and lying flat, with each pea hanging from the seam on a short stalk.
setup.caption: 2. Open a pod along the seam. Leave the seeds on their stalks.

setup.art: A close view through a hand lens of the end of an open pea pod: one full pea, and beside it two tiny flat pale grains on short stalks.
setup.caption: 3. Look for tiny pale grains on stalks. Each one is an empty place.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for pods, and columns of small numbers for full seeds, empty places and ovules.
setup.caption: 4. Count the full seeds and the empty places in every pod.

flow.do: 1. Put 20 pods on a plate, without choosing the fattest. 2. Look at one closed pod together. Find the green cap at the stalk end, and the thin dry point at the other end. 3. Ask the questions below. Write the guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: This pod grew from the ovary of one flower. The green cap is the old sepals. The dry point at the tip is what is left of the style. How many ovules do you think one pod began with? Has every one grown into a seed? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at one closed pod. Find the green cap and the dry tip. Guess how many seeds are inside. Guess if every place is full. Say why you think so.

ask.q: Do you think every ovule in a pod becomes a seed? Why?
good: Yes, because they all get the same water and food from the plant.
No, because some may not have got any pollen.
I am not sure. We need to open many pods to know.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect every place to be full, because pods in a shop look full from outside.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Empty Places Test. You look at a closed pod and guess what is inside.

flow.do: 1. Open the first pod. Press the seam near the tip until it splits, and run a thumb along the seam. 2. Do not pull the seeds off. Each seed hangs from the seam on a short stalk. 3. Look between the seeds and at both ends for tiny pale grains on stalks. Use a hand lens or a phone camera.
flow.say: Look along the seam. Each seed hangs on a short stalk. Now look for very small, flat, pale grains on stalks of the same kind. What do you think they are?
flow.kid: Open one pod along the seam. Leave the seeds on their stalks. Look for tiny pale grains on stalks. What could they be?

ask.q: What do you think the tiny pale grains are?
good: Seeds that did not grow.
Ovules that were never fertilised.
Young seeds that stopped growing.

flow.parent: The tiny grains are ovules that never grew into seeds. In a pea pod they are as small as a pinhead or a mustard seed. They often sit at the two ends. We call each one an empty place. If the first five pods show no empty places, take shorter, thinner or bent pods for the rest. Write that you did so.
flow.context: In this step of the Empty Places Test you open the first pod and look for ovules that never grew.

flow.do: 1. Draw the results table with 20 rows. 2. Open each pod in the same way. Count the full seeds and the empty places, and add them to get the ovules. 3. For each empty place, write the position: stalk end, middle or tip end.
flow.say: Now we count all 20 pods in the same way. For each pod, count the full seeds and the empty places. Then write where the empty places were.
flow.kid: Open each pod the same way. Count the full seeds. Count the empty places. Write where the empty places were.

ask.q: Why do we open 20 pods, and not just 2?
good: Two pods could both be unusual.
With 20 pods we can see what usually happens.
Pods differ, so we need many to find a pattern.

check.q: A pod has 6 full seeds and 2 empty places. How many ovules did the ovary of that flower hold?
check.why: Every seed and every empty place began as one ovule, so 6 + 2 = 8 ovules. Choosing 6 means counting only the ovules that grew, and leaving out the ones that did not.

flow.context: In this step of the Empty Places Test you count the seeds and the empty places in all 20 pods.

flow.do: 1. Add up the full seeds in all 20 pods. Add up the ovules in all 20 pods. 2. Divide the seeds by the ovules. This is the share of ovules that became seeds. 3. Count the pods with no empty place. 4. Add up the empty places at the stalk end, in the middle and at the tip end.
flow.say: Add up all the seeds and all the ovules. What share of the ovules became seeds? How many pods were completely full? Where were the empty places most often?
flow.kid: Add up the seeds. Add up the ovules. Divide the seeds by the ovules. Count the pods that were full. Where were most of the empty places?
flow.parent: A worked example: 132 seeds from 160 ovules is 132 ÷ 160 = 0.825. That is about 83 percent, or about 5 ovules in every 6. A calculator is fine for the division.
flow.context: In this step of the Empty Places Test you add up the 20 pods. You find the share of ovules that became seeds.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 2. Then read the note below together. 3. Ask the questions.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: All the ovules in one pod had the same mother plant, the same water and the same light. So why did some not grow?
good: Each ovule needs their own pollen tube, and some did not get one.
Some may have been fertilised, and then the plant stopped feeding them.

ask.q: Was any pod thin or pinched at the place where a seed was missing?
good: Yes, the pod was narrow there.
No, I could not see a difference.

flow.parent: Most pods have at least one empty place. The share of ovules that became seeds is often between 70 and 95 percent. Write down what you really found, even if it differs. The reason: each ovule is fertilised separately, by one pollen tube. An ovule that no tube reached stays tiny. Some ovules are fertilised and then stop growing, because the plant sends the food to other seeds. You cannot tell these two apart by looking. In many pods the empty places are commonest at the two ends, but pods differ.
flow.think: A farmer wants every pod full. What would have to happen in the field at flowering time?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Empty Places Test. You say what you found in the 20 pods, and why some ovules did not become seeds.

experiments.title: The Pollen Rain Test: how much wind-blown pollen lands on a small stigma and on a big one?
experiments.context: In this experiment 100 moong seeds are pollen grains blown by the wind. You let them fall like rain over two catchers: a small katori and a wide bowl. You count how many land in each, to see how much pollen the wind wastes.
experiments.question: When pollen falls by chance, how many grains out of 100 land on a small stigma? How many land on a stigma three times as wide?
experiments.predict: The wide bowl is three times as wide as the katori. Guess how many of 100 seeds will land in the katori, and how many in the wide bowl. Why do you think so? Write both guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Both catchers stand in the same rain, at the same distance from the centre mark. The person who drops the seeds keeps their eyes shut, so they cannot aim. The catchers swap sides after each run. Chance decides where each seed falls, so you do three runs and add them up.

materials.item: whole moong seeds, counted into a tumbler
small steel katori, about 7 centimetres across
wide bowl, deep plate or kadai, about 21 centimetres across (three times as wide as the katori)
bedsheet or large towel to spread on the floor
small pieces of cloth, to line the katori and the wide bowl so that seeds do not bounce out
ruler, and a coin for the centre mark

experiments.record: Fill in one row for each of the three runs. Add up each column. Then write how many times as many seeds the wide bowl caught as the katori. Last, do the visitor run and write its result under the table.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: seeds caught out of 300 dropped, over three runs
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your own numbers will differ, because chance decides where each seed falls.

setup.art: A bedsheet on the floor with a coin in the middle, a small steel katori on one side of the coin and a wide bowl on the other side, each lined with a piece of cloth.
setup.caption: 1. Put the katori and the wide bowl 30 centimetres from the coin, on opposite sides.

setup.art: A child standing over the coin with eyes shut, holding a tumbler at chest height and shaking moong seeds out of it in small circles.
setup.caption: 2. Shut your eyes. Shake out 100 seeds from chest height, moving the tumbler in circles.

setup.art: Moong seeds scattered over the sheet, with a few in the wide bowl and one in the katori, and a hand counting them.
setup.caption: 3. Count the seeds in each catcher. Do three runs.

flow.do: 1. Spread the sheet on the floor and put a coin in the middle. 2. Line the katori and the wide bowl with cloth. Put each one 30 centimetres from the coin, on opposite sides. 3. Measure how wide each catcher is. 4. Ask for the two guesses and the reasons, and write them.
flow.say: The moong seeds are pollen grains in the wind. The katori is a small stigma. The bowl is a stigma three times as wide. Out of 100 grains, how many will land in each? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The seeds are pollen in the wind. The katori is a small stigma. The bowl is three times as wide. Guess how many seeds land in each. Say why.

ask.q: The bowl is three times as wide as the katori. How many times as many seeds do you think the bowl will catch? Why?
good: Three times as many, because the bowl is three times as wide.
More than three times, because the bowl is bigger in every direction.
I am not sure. Chance decides where they fall.

flow.parent: Many children guess three times as many. Do not correct this. The count will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pollen Rain Test. You set out a small catcher and a wide catcher, and guess how many seeds each will catch.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands over the coin and holds the tumbler of 100 seeds at chest height. 2. With eyes shut, they shake the seeds out slowly. They move the tumbler in circles about as wide as a dinner plate. 3. Count the seeds in each catcher and write the numbers. 4. Collect all 100 seeds. Swap the two catchers, and do runs 2 and 3.
flow.say: Shut your eyes, so that you cannot aim. Shake the seeds out slowly, and move the tumbler in circles. Then we count what each stigma caught.
flow.kid: Stand over the coin. Shut your eyes. Shake the seeds out slowly in circles. Count the seeds in each catcher. Do this three times.

ask.q: Why must your eyes be shut?
good: So that I cannot aim at a catcher.
The wind does not aim, so I should not aim.

check.q: In the Pollen Rain Test, why do the katori and the wide bowl swap sides after each run?
options: So one side cannot favour one catcher
check.why: A person may shake a little more to one side without knowing it. Swapping the catchers shares that out between them. Then a difference in the counts comes from the size of the catcher.

flow.context: In this step of the Pollen Rain Test you drop 100 seeds three times and count how many each catcher holds.

flow.do: 1. Now be a visitor. Pick up 10 seeds in your fingers. 2. Walk to the katori and put the seeds in. 3. Write how many of the 10 arrived.
flow.say: A bee does not drop pollen from the sky. She carries pollen from flower to flower. Carry 10 seeds straight to the katori. How many arrive?
flow.kid: Now you are a bee. Pick up 10 seeds. Carry them to the katori. How many arrived?
flow.context: In this step of the Pollen Rain Test you carry seeds to the small catcher by hand. An animal visitor carries pollen to a stigma in the same way.

flow.do: 1. Add up each column of the table. 2. Divide the wide bowl's total by the katori's total. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 4. Then read the note below together.
flow.say: Add up the three runs. How many times as many seeds did the wide bowl catch? Now say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Add up the three runs. Compare the bowl with the katori. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Out of 300 seeds dropped, how many missed both catchers?
good: Most of them.
More than 250.

ask.q: The visitor carried 10 seeds and the rain dropped 300. Which put more seeds in the katori?
good: The visitor, with far fewer seeds.
The visitor put in 10. The rain put in only a few.

flow.parent: The katori usually catches 0 to 4 seeds in a run, and the wide bowl about 5 to 25. The numbers jump about, because the katori's count is so small. Over three runs the wide bowl usually catches many more than three times as many. A bowl three times as wide covers nine times as much floor, because 3 × 3 = 9. If the katori caught nothing at all, write that the bowl caught all the seeds that were caught. The reason for the waste: wind-blown pollen lands by chance, and a small stigma covers very little space. So wind flowers make huge amounts of pollen, and their stigmas are long and feathery to cover more space. An animal visitor delivers pollen straight to the stigma, so a visitor flower needs far less pollen.
flow.think: A maize cob has about 500 silks. If only 1 pollen grain in 100 lands on a silk, how many grains must fall near that cob?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Pollen Rain Test. You compare how many seeds the small catcher and the wide catcher caught, and compare the rain with carrying.

activities.title: Take a Flower Apart: find the four rings in a hibiscus
activities.context: In this activity you take one hibiscus flower apart from the outside in. You find the four rings of parts, count each ring, and cut the ovary open to see the ovules.

materials.item: single red hibiscus flowers with five petals, from a plant, a neighbour or a flower seller. If you cannot get hibiscus, use a lily, a tuberose, a bhindi flower or a gulmohar flower
sheet of white paper with four circles drawn one inside the other
sticky tape
piece of dark cloth or dark paper, to see the pollen
hand lens, or a phone camera that can zoom
small knife or blade, used by a grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the ovary. Wash hands afterwards. Do not use oleander (arali or kaner) or datura flowers, which are poisonous. If pollen makes your child sneeze, do not sniff the flower closely.
activities.record: Tape the parts onto the four circles: sepals on the outer circle, then petals, then stamens, and the carpels in the middle. Fill in a flower table with four rows: the ring, the name of the part, how many, and what the part does.

example_chart.title: The four rings of a hibiscus flower, from the outside in
rows: More than 50, joined in a tube
5 joined: 5 stigmas, 1 style, 1 ovary with 5 chambers
example_chart.show: The four rings of parts in a hibiscus flower, with the number of parts in each ring.
example_chart.note: A hibiscus also has a ring of thin green leaves below the sepals. That extra ring belongs to the hibiscus family. Leave it out of the table.

setup.art: A red hibiscus flower lying on white paper beside four circles drawn one inside the other.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the whole flower. Draw four circles on paper.

setup.art: Five green sepals and five red petals taped onto the two outer circles, with the long red column of the flower lying beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Take off the sepals, then the petals. Tape them on the two outer circles.

setup.art: A close view of the hibiscus column: many small yellow anthers on short stalks along a red tube, and five round red pads at the tip.
setup.caption: 3. Find the stamens along the tube, and the five stigmas at the tip.

setup.art: A small green ovary cut across, seen through a hand lens, showing five chambers with tiny white dots.
setup.caption: 4. A grown-up cuts the ovary across. Look for the chambers and the ovules.

flow.do: 1. Put one flower on the table and keep the second as a spare. 2. Look at the flower from the side, without taking anything off. 3. Ask the questions below, and write the guess.
flow.say: Look at the whole flower before we open it. How many different kinds of parts can you see? Which part do you think makes the seeds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the whole flower. How many kinds of parts can you see? Which part makes the seeds? Say why you think so.

ask.q: Which part of this flower do you think makes the seeds? Why?
good: The yellow dots, because they look like tiny seeds.
The bottom of the flower, because fruits grow where the flower was.
The long red stick in the middle.

flow.parent: Many children point to the yellow anthers, because pollen looks like tiny seeds. Leave the guess as it is for now.
flow.context: This is the first step of Take a Flower Apart. You look at a whole hibiscus flower and guess which part makes the seeds.

flow.do: 1. Peel off the thin green leaves at the very base, and put them aside. 2. Under them is a green cup with 5 points. These are the sepals. Tear the cup open and count the points. 3. Pull off the petals one at a time, at the base, and count them. 4. Tape the sepals and the petals on the two outer circles.
flow.say: Start from the outside. The green cup is the sepals. They covered the bud. Count the points. Then take off the petals one by one and count them.
flow.kid: Peel off the thin green leaves. Find the green cup. Count the points. Pull off the petals one by one. Count them and tape them down.

ask.q: The petals are large and red. The sepals are small and green. What does that tell you about their jobs?
good: The petals are there to be seen by visitors.
The sepals only had to cover the bud.

flow.parent: The petals of a hibiscus are joined at the base to the red column. Pull each petal gently sideways, so that the column stays whole.
flow.context: In this step of Take a Flower Apart you remove and count the two outer rings, the sepals and the petals.

flow.do: 1. Look at the long red column. Along it are many short stalks, each with a yellow head. Each one is a stamen. 2. Dab a yellow head on the dark cloth, and look at the pollen with the lens. 3. Look at the very tip of the column. Count the round pads there. These are the stigmas. Touch one gently.
flow.say: Each yellow head is an anther, on a short stalk called a filament. Dab one on the dark cloth. What comes off? Now look at the tip. How many round pads are there? How do they feel?
flow.kid: Find the yellow heads along the column. Dab one on the dark cloth. Look at the pollen. Count the round pads at the tip. Touch one gently.

ask.q: The stigmas stand beyond the anthers, at the very tip. What will a visitor touch first as she lands?
good: The stigmas.
She touches the stigmas first, with pollen from the last flower she visited.

flow.parent: There are 5 stigmas, and they feel velvety and slightly sticky. There are too many stamens to count quickly: more than 50. Pick off a few stamens and tape them on the third circle.
flow.context: In this step of Take a Flower Apart you find the stamens and the stigmas on the column of the hibiscus.

flow.do: 1. Slit the red tube lengthwise with a fingernail. Inside is a thin pale thread, the style. 2. Follow the style down to a small green swelling at the base of the flower. This is the ovary. 3. A grown-up cuts the ovary across the middle. 4. Look at the cut face with the lens or the phone camera. Count the chambers, and look for tiny white dots.
flow.say: The stamens are joined in a tube. Inside the tube is the style. Follow it down. What do you find at the bottom? Now look at the cut ovary. How many chambers? What is inside them?
flow.kid: Slit the red tube with a fingernail. Find the thin thread inside. Follow the thread down to the green swelling. Ask a grown-up to cut it. Count the chambers.

ask.q: There are 5 stigmas at the top and 5 chambers in the ovary. What does that suggest?
good: The female part is 5 carpels joined together.
Each stigma belongs to one chamber.

flow.parent: The ovary is about half a centimetre wide. The white dots in the chambers are the ovules. They are very small, so use the phone camera's zoom if the lens is not strong enough. Tape the style, with the stigmas and one half of the ovary, in the middle circle.
flow.context: In this step of Take a Flower Apart you find the style and the ovary. A grown-up cuts the ovary open.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the flower table together: ring, part, how many, what the part does. 2. Go back to the first guess about which part makes the seeds. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Fill in the table from the outside in. Then look at your first guess. Which part holds the ovules that can become seeds? Were you right?
flow.kid: Fill in the flower table. Look at your first guess. Which part holds the ovules? Answer the question.

check.q: In which part of a flower are the ovules found?
check.why: The ovules are sealed inside the ovary, at the base of the carpel. The anthers hold pollen grains, which carry the male cells. Choosing the anthers usually means taking pollen grains for tiny seeds.

flow.context: This is the last step of Take a Flower Apart. You fill in a table of the four rings and check your first guess.

activities.title: Count the Carpels: read the chambers in six kitchen fruits
activities.context: In this activity you cut six fruits from the kitchen across the middle and count the chambers. Each chamber grew from one carpel of the flower, so the fruit shows how many carpels the flower had.

materials.item: bhindi
tomato
cucumber
banana
lemon or orange
capsicum or large green chilli
knife and chopping board, used by a grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. The cut fruits can all be cooked or eaten afterwards.
activities.record: Make a table with four columns: the fruit, your guess, the chambers you counted, and where the seeds are attached. Draw the cut face of two of the fruits.

example_chart.title: Chambers usually found in six fruits
rows: 2 to 5, or many in a large tomato
example_chart.show: Six kitchen fruits, each cut across the middle, with the number of chambers that are usually found.
example_chart.note: Fruits of one kind can differ. Write the number that you really count.

setup.art: Six whole fruits in a row on a chopping board: a bhindi, a tomato, a cucumber, a banana, a lemon and a capsicum.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the six fruits. Guess how many chambers each has inside.

setup.art: A bhindi cut across the middle, showing five chambers like a star, each with white seeds.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts each fruit across the middle. Count the chambers.

setup.art: A banana cut across, showing three faint parts and tiny dark specks near the centre.
setup.caption: 3. Look closely at the banana. Find the three parts and the dark specks.

flow.do: 1. Line up the six fruits. 2. Say that each grew from the ovary of one flower. 3. Ask your child to guess the number of chambers in each fruit, and to say why. Write the guesses.
flow.say: Each of these grew from the ovary of one flower. An ovary can have one chamber or several. How many chambers do you think each fruit has? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each fruit grew from one ovary. Guess how many chambers each fruit has. Say why. Write your guesses.
flow.parent: If you have done Take a Flower Apart, remind your child that the hibiscus ovary had 5 chambers. Bhindi belongs to the hibiscus family.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Carpels. You guess how many chambers six kitchen fruits have inside.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts each fruit across the middle. 2. Your child counts the chambers on the cut face, and writes the number. 3. In each fruit, look at where the seeds are attached.
flow.say: Count the chambers on the cut face. In a lemon, count the segments. Where are the seeds attached in each fruit: to the middle, or to the wall?
flow.kid: Count the chambers in each fruit. Count the segments in the lemon. Look at where the seeds are attached. Write the numbers.

ask.q: The bhindi has 5 chambers and the cucumber has 3. What does that tell you about their flowers?
good: The bhindi flower had 5 carpels joined together.
The cucumber flower had 3 carpels.

flow.parent: Each chamber grew from one carpel. In the banana the three parts are faint: press the cut end gently and it splits into three. The tiny dark specks near the centre are ovules that never grew into seeds.
flow.context: In this step of Count the Carpels a grown-up cuts each fruit across, and you count the chambers.

flow.do: 1. Compare the counts with the guesses. 2. Draw the cut face of two fruits, and label one chamber and one seed. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Which count surprised you most? Now draw two of the cut faces. Label one chamber and one seed on each.
flow.kid: Compare your counts with your guesses. Draw two cut faces. Label one chamber and one seed.

ask.q: The banana has three parts and tiny dark specks, but no seeds. What are the specks?
good: Ovules that never grew.
The banana grew without fertilisation, so the ovules stayed tiny.

ask.q: A cook calls bhindi, tomato and cucumber vegetables. Why does a botanist call them fruits?
good: They grew from the ovary of a flower.
They hold seeds.

check.q: An orange has 10 segments. How many carpels did the ovary of the orange flower have?
check.why: Each segment of an orange grew from one carpel, so 10 segments mean 10 carpels joined together. Choosing 1 means counting the whole fruit as one carpel. A pea pod has 1 carpel, but an orange has many.

flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Carpels. You compare your counts with your guesses and draw two of the fruits.

activities.title: The Hidden Journey: draw how a pollen grain reaches an ovule
activities.context: In this activity you draw what you think happens after a pollen grain lands on a stigma. Then you read what scientists saw under the microscope, and draw it again. Last, you work out how long the journey is for a grain of maize pollen.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper
pencil and two colour pencils
ruler

activities.record: Keep both drawings side by side. On the second drawing, label seven parts: pollen grain, stigma, style, pollen tube, ovary, ovule and egg cell. Write the scale sum under it.

setup.art: A large outline of one carpel on paper, shaped like a long-necked bottle, with one dot on the top and a few small circles at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a large carpel. Put one pollen grain on the stigma and four ovules in the ovary.

setup.art: A child drawing arrows and question marks between the dot at the top and the circles at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your own idea of how the pollen starts a seed.

setup.art: A second drawing of the carpel, with a thin coloured line growing from the pollen grain down through the style to one ovule.
setup.caption: 3. After reading, draw the pollen tube from the grain to one ovule.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a carpel as tall as the page: a stigma, a long style and an ovary. 2. They draw one pollen grain on the stigma and four ovules in the ovary. 3. Ask the question below. Your child draws their own idea on the picture.
flow.say: The pollen grain is up here on the stigma. The ovules are down here, sealed inside the ovary. A seed cannot begin until something from the pollen reaches an ovule. How do you think that happens? Draw your idea.
flow.kid: Draw a tall carpel. Put a pollen grain on top. Put four ovules at the bottom. How does the pollen reach an ovule? Draw your idea.

ask.q: How do you think the pollen reaches the ovules?
good: The pollen grain falls down a hole in the style.
The pollen sends something down.
The ovule climbs up.
The pollen grows down.

flow.parent: Any idea with a reason is welcome. Scientists themselves once thought that pollen sent a vapour down the style.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hidden Journey. You draw your own idea of how pollen on a stigma starts a seed inside the ovary.

flow.do: 1. Read the note below to your child. 2. On a new sheet, your child draws the carpel again. 3. This time they draw the pollen tube in colour, from the grain to one ovule. They add two male cells near the tip. 4. They label the seven parts.
flow.say: Here is what scientists saw. The pollen grain grows a tube, thinner than a hair. The tube grows down through the style and into one ovule. Two male cells travel inside it. One joins the egg cell. Now draw that.
flow.kid: The pollen grain grows a thin tube. The tube grows down to one ovule. Draw the tube in colour. Label the seven parts.

ask.q: There are four ovules in your drawing and one pollen grain. How many seeds can form?
good: One. Each ovule needs their own pollen tube.
One seed, and three empty places.

flow.parent: The seven labels are: pollen grain, stigma, style, pollen tube, ovary, ovule and egg cell. The style has no hole down the middle in most flowers. The tube pushes between the cells and takes food from them as it grows.
flow.context: In this step of the Hidden Journey you draw the pollen tube that scientists saw under the microscope.

flow.do: 1. Give your child these two numbers. A maize pollen grain is one tenth of a millimetre wide. A maize silk can be 20 centimetres long. 2. Your child works out how many times the grain's own width the tube must grow. 3. Then they scale it up: if the grain were a marble 1 centimetre wide, how long would the tube be?
flow.say: A maize pollen grain is one tenth of a millimetre wide. The silk is 20 centimetres long. How many grain-widths long is the tube? If the grain were a marble, how far would the tube reach?
flow.kid: A maize pollen grain is one tenth of a millimetre wide. The silk is 20 centimetres long. How many grain-widths is that? Work it out.
flow.parent: 20 centimetres is 200 millimetres. 200 ÷ 0.1 = 2,000, so the tube grows 2,000 times the width of the grain. A marble 1 centimetre wide would need a tube 2,000 centimetres long. That is 20 metres, about as long as two city buses end to end.

check.q: What does a pollen tube carry down to the ovule?
check.why: The tube carries two male cells from the pollen grain. One of them joins the egg cell, and that is fertilisation. Choosing a tiny seed is the old idea that the young plant comes ready-made in the pollen.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Hidden Journey. You work out how far a maize pollen tube grows, compared with the width of the pollen grain.

activities.title: Wind or Visitor? Read the clues on eight Indian flowers
activities.context: In this activity you read a table of eight flowers that grow in India. From the features of each flower, you work out whether the wind or an animal carries the pollen.

materials.item: the table of eight flowers below
notebook and pencil
a flowering grass stalk from a pavement or a lawn, and a sheet of dark paper (if you can find one)

activities.record: For each flower write 'wind' or 'animal', and the two clues that decided your answer. If you say 'animal', guess which kind of animal.

example_chart.title: Eight flowers and their features
rows: Hang outside on thin stalks. Much dry pollen
In the tassel at the top. Millions of light grains
Long silk threads with fine hairs
On a column. Sticky, spiky pollen
Large and yellow, open at dawn
Large and sticky, in separate flowers
example_chart.show: Eight flowers, with the features of the petals, scent, nectar, pollen and stigma of each.
example_chart.note: The coconut is the hard one. Bees visit the flowers for nectar, and the wind also carries the pollen.

setup.art: A table of eight flowers with small drawings of each: paddy, maize, hibiscus, tuberose, pumpkin, red silk cotton, grass and coconut.
setup.caption: 1. Read the features of the eight flowers.

setup.art: A notebook page with two headings, Wind and Animal, and flower names being written under each with a clue beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Sort the flowers into wind and animal. Write two clues for each.

setup.art: A child shaking a flowering grass stalk over a sheet of dark paper, with fine pale dust falling on the paper.
setup.caption: 3. If you find a grass in flower, shake the stalk over dark paper.

flow.do: 1. Read the first two rows of the table together. 2. Ask what a flower would need in order to use the wind. Ask what a flower would need in order to bring an animal. 3. Write your child's two lists.
flow.say: Some flowers use the wind to carry pollen. Others use animals. What would a flower need for the wind? What would a flower need to bring an animal? Why?
flow.kid: Some flowers use wind. Some use animals. What does a wind flower need? What does a visitor flower need? Say why.

ask.q: Would a wind flower need bright petals? Why or why not?
good: No. The wind cannot see.
No. Petals would cost food and might block the wind.

flow.context: This is the first step of Wind or Visitor. You think about what a flower needs for each way of moving pollen.

flow.do: 1. Your child reads each of the eight rows. 2. For each flower they write 'wind' or 'animal', with two clues. 3. For the animal flowers, they guess the kind of animal.
flow.say: Read each flower's features. Decide: wind or animal? Write the two clues that helped you most. For an animal flower, guess who comes.
flow.kid: Read each row. Write wind or animal. Write two clues. For an animal flower, guess who visits.
flow.parent: Paddy, maize and doob grass: wind. Hibiscus: animals, mostly butterflies and birds. Tuberose: moths, because the flower is white and scented at night. Pumpkin: bees. Red silk cotton tree: birds, because the flower is red, with much nectar and little scent. Coconut: both bees and wind.
flow.context: In this step of Wind or Visitor you sort eight flowers by how their pollen is carried.

flow.do: 1. Check the answers together. 2. Ask which flower was hardest to place, and why. 3. If you have a flowering grass stalk, shake it over dark paper and look for pollen. 4. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which flower was hardest to place? Why? Some flowers use both the wind and animals. Which one in the table does?
flow.kid: Check your answers. Which flower was hardest? If you have a grass stalk, shake it over dark paper.

ask.q: A wind flower makes far more pollen than a visitor flower. Why?
good: Most wind-blown pollen never lands on a stigma.
The wind does not aim, so most is wasted.

flow.parent: A grass in flower shows small anthers hanging out on threads. Not every stalk is shedding pollen on the day you pick it, so you may see no dust.

check.q: A flower is white, opens in the evening and has a strong scent at night. Who most likely carries the pollen?
check.why: White shows up in dim light, and a strong scent at night guides moths, who fly then. A wind flower has no need of scent. Sunbirds feed by day and find flowers mostly by colour.

flow.context: This is the last step of Wind or Visitor. You check your sorting and look at the flower that uses both ways.

activities.title: One Silk, One Kernel: follow the threads on a maize cob (if you can get a cob in its husk)
activities.context: In this activity you open a maize cob that still has the green husk and the silk threads. You follow single silks to see where they end, and you count the kernels and the bare places.

materials.item: maize cob (bhutta or sweet corn) still in the green husk, with the silk threads at the tip
steel plate
notebook and pencil

activities.record: Write the number of rows, the number of kernels in one row, and the estimate of kernels on the cob. Write the number of bare places you counted, and where on the cob they were.

setup.art: A maize cob in the green husk with a tuft of brown silk threads at the tip, lying on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the closed cob. Guess how many kernels and how many silks it has.

setup.art: A hand peeling back one husk leaf to show silk threads lying flat along the rows of kernels.
setup.caption: 2. Peel the husk leaf by leaf. Leave the silks lying on the cob.

setup.art: A fingernail following a single silk thread down between two rows to one kernel.
setup.caption: 3. Follow one silk to the end. Where does the silk stop?

flow.do: 1. Look at the closed cob together. 2. Ask your child to guess the number of kernels, and the number of silk threads. 3. Ask what the threads might be for, and why. Write the guesses.
flow.say: This cob is the female part of a maize plant. How many kernels do you think are inside? How many silk threads? What do you think the threads are for? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the closed cob. Guess how many kernels are inside. Guess how many threads. What are the threads for? Say why.
flow.parent: Street sellers sell maize cobs in the husk during the rains. Many shops sell sweet corn in the husk all year. If the seller has already removed the husk, ask for one that is whole.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Silk, One Kernel. You guess how many kernels and silk threads a maize cob has.

flow.do: 1. Peel the husk off one leaf at a time. Try to leave the silks lying on the cob. 2. Pick one silk near the tip and follow it down with a fingernail. See where it ends. 3. Do this with five more silks.
flow.say: Peel slowly, so that the silks stay in place. Now follow one silk down. Where does it end? Follow five more. Does any kernel have two silks?
flow.kid: Peel the husk slowly. Follow one thread down with your fingernail. Where does the thread end? Follow five more threads.

ask.q: Where did each silk end?
good: At one kernel.
Each silk went to a different kernel.

flow.parent: Each silk is joined to one kernel, usually at the top of the kernel. On a cooked or old cob the silks break easily, so a fresh cob works best. Each silk is the style of one ovule.
flow.context: In this step of One Silk, One Kernel you follow single silk threads down the cob. You see where each one ends.

flow.do: 1. Count the rows of kernels round the cob. 2. Count the kernels in one row. Multiply the two numbers. 3. Look for bare places, where a tiny flat dot sits in the place of a kernel. Count them, and write where they are.
flow.say: Count the rows round the cob. Count the kernels in one row. Multiply them. Now look for bare places. Where on the cob are most of them?
flow.kid: Count the rows. Count the kernels in one row. Multiply. Look for bare places. Where are they?

ask.q: Each bare place had a silk too. Why did no kernel grow there?
good: That silk did not catch a pollen grain.
No pollen tube reached that ovule.

flow.parent: A cob usually has 12 to 18 rows, and the number of rows is always even. With about 30 to 40 kernels in a row, a cob holds about 400 to 600 kernels. Bare places are commonest at the tip. The silks from the tip come out last, when the tassels may have finished shedding pollen.

check.q: A maize cob has 480 kernels and 20 bare places. How many silks did the young cob have?
check.why: Every ovule on the cob has one silk, whether a kernel grew or not. 480 + 20 = 500 ovules, so 500 silks. Choosing 480 leaves out the silks that caught no pollen.

flow.context: This is the last step of One Silk, One Kernel. You estimate the kernels on the cob and look for the places where no kernel grew.

activities.title: The Marigold Count: is a marigold one flower or many?
activities.context: In this activity you pull one marigold apart and count the pieces. You look at one piece closely. Then you decide whether a marigold is one flower with many petals, or a head of many small flowers.

materials.item: marigold, from a garland or a flower seller
steel plate
hand lens, or a phone camera that can zoom
notebook and pencil

activities.record: Write your guess and your count. Draw one piece of the marigold as large as your hand, and label the petal, the ovary and the forked stigma.

setup.art: A whole orange marigold on a steel plate beside a notebook with a guess written in it.
setup.caption: 1. Guess how many petals the marigold has.

setup.art: A marigold pulled apart on a plate, with the orange pieces arranged in heaps of ten.
setup.caption: 2. Pull the marigold apart. Put the pieces in heaps of ten.

setup.art: One piece of a marigold drawn large: an orange strap at the top, a forked thread, and a thin pale stick at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Look at one piece closely. Find the thin pale part at the bottom.

flow.do: 1. Put the marigold on the plate. 2. Ask your child how many petals it has, and whether it is one flower. 3. Write the guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: Is this one flower? How many petals do you think it has? Where do you think the ovary is? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Is this one flower? Guess how many petals. Guess where the ovary is. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Marigold Count. You guess how many petals a marigold has, and where the ovary is.

flow.do: 1. Hold the green cup at the base and pull the orange pieces out, a few at a time. 2. Put them in heaps of ten, and count the heaps. 3. Pick up one piece and look at it from top to bottom with the lens.
flow.say: Pull the pieces out gently, so that each one comes out whole. Make heaps of ten. Now look at one piece. What is at the bottom of it?
flow.kid: Pull the pieces out gently. Make heaps of ten. Count the heaps. Look at one piece from top to bottom.

ask.q: What do you see at the bottom of each orange piece?
good: A thin pale stick.
A small white part, like a tiny seed.
A forked thread coming out of the tube.

flow.parent: A marigold from a garland often has more than 100 pieces. Each piece has an orange petal at the top. At the bottom is a thin pale stick about 1 centimetre long, which is an ovary with one ovule inside. In many pieces a thin thread with a forked tip stands out of the petal. That is the style, with two stigmas.
flow.context: In this step of the Marigold Count you pull the marigold apart, count the pieces and look closely at one.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws one piece large, and labels the petal, the ovary and the forked stigma. 2. Ask whether each piece is a petal or a whole flower, and why. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Each piece has a petal, a stigma and an ovary of its own. So is each piece a petal, or a whole small flower? How many flowers were in your marigold?
flow.kid: Draw one piece large. Label the petal, the ovary and the stigma. Is each piece a petal or a flower? Say why.

ask.q: Is each piece a petal or a flower? What is your evidence?
good: A flower, because each piece has an ovary and a stigma of its own.
A petal has no ovary, so these are flowers.

flow.parent: Each piece is a whole small flower. A marigold is a head of many flowers, and so are a sunflower and a chrysanthemum. Dry an old marigold for a week and pull it apart. Each ovary has become a thin black fruit with one seed inside. These are the marigold 'seeds' that gardeners sow.

check.q: A sunflower head makes about 1,000 seeds. What does that tell you about the head?
options: It had one very large ovary
check.why: Each sunflower seed grows from the ovary of one small flower in the head. About 1,000 seeds mean about 1,000 small flowers. Choosing one large ovary treats the head as a single flower.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Marigold Count. You decide whether each piece of a marigold is a petal or a whole small flower.

projects.title: The Bag Test: does this plant need a visitor to make fruit? (if you have a plant in flower)
projects.context: In this 15-day project you cover five flower buds with small net bags, so that no insect can reach them. You leave five other buds open. Then you count how many flowers of each group grow into fruits. Charles Darwin tested clover in the same way.
projects.question: Can the flowers of this plant make fruit when no visitor can reach them? Or do they need pollen brought from outside?
projects.predict: Five buds will be covered with net bags and five will be left open. How many of each five do you think will grow into fruits? Why do you think so? Write both numbers and your reasons.

materials.item: potted or garden plant with at least 10 flower buds: chilli, tomato, brinjal, bhindi, beans, balsam, or a pumpkin, gourd or cucumber vine
small bags, about 10 centimetres square, sewn or tied from an old net curtain, mosquito net or thin muslin
pieces of thread in two colours, each about 15 centimetres long
notebook and pencil

projects.safety: Ask before you use a neighbour's plant. Tie the bags loosely, so that the stalk is not squeezed. Wash hands after touching chilli plants.

schedule.what: Predict. Choose 10 buds that have not opened. Bag 5 and tie one colour of thread below each. Tie the other colour below 5 open buds.
Look at all 10. Write which flowers have opened. Do not open the bags.
When the petals of a bagged flower have dried or fallen, take that bag off. Write the date.
Look at the base of each flower. Write 'swelling', 'no change' or 'fallen off' for each of the 10.
Count the fruits in each group. Write a conclusion.

projects.record: Make a table with 10 rows, one for each bud. Write the group (bagged or open), and what you see on days 3, 6, 10 and 15. On day 15, write the number of fruits out of 5 in each group. Then write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
projects.fair_test: All 10 buds are on the same plant, or on plants of the same kind standing together. All are closed when you start. Only one thing differs: whether a visitor can reach the flower. Five flowers in each group is a small number, so a difference of one fruit means little.

setup.art: A chilli plant in a pot with several closed flower buds, and a child tying a red thread below one bud.
setup.caption: 1. Choose 10 closed buds. Tie one colour of thread below 5 of them.

setup.art: A small white net bag tied loosely over a flower bud on a plant, with a blue thread tied below the bag.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the other 5 buds with net bags, and tie the second colour below each.

setup.art: The same plant some days later: an open flower with a bee beside the flower, and a bagged flower with dried petals inside the net.
setup.caption: 3. When a bagged flower's petals have dried, take the bag off.

setup.art: Two small green chillies on stalks with red threads and two more on stalks with blue threads, and a notebook table beside the pot.
setup.caption: 4. On day 15, count the fruits in each group.

flow.do: 1. Find 10 buds that have not opened. 2. Slip a net bag over each of 5 buds, and tie the mouth loosely round the stalk. Tie one colour of thread below each. 3. Tie the other colour of thread below the 5 open buds. 4. Ask for the prediction and the reasons. Write them.
flow.say: Five buds are covered, so no bee, fly or butterfly can reach them. Five are open. How many of each five will grow into fruits? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find 10 closed buds. Put net bags on 5. Tie thread on all 10. Guess how many of each 5 will make fruit. Say why.

ask.q: How many of the bagged flowers do you think will make fruit? Why?
good: None, because no insect can bring pollen.
Some, because the flower's own pollen is right there.
All of them, because fruit just grows after a flower.

flow.parent: The bag must go on before the bud opens. A flower that has already opened may have been visited. On a pumpkin, gourd or cucumber vine, bag and tag only the female buds. A female bud has a tiny fruit below the flower.
flow.wait: Look at the flowers again in 2 days
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bag Test. You cover five buds with net bags, leave five open, and predict how many will make fruit.

flow.do: 1. Look at all 10 flowers without opening any bag. 2. Write which have opened. 3. Watch the open flowers for five minutes, and write any visitor you see.
flow.say: Which flowers have opened? Sit still for five minutes. Does anyone visit the open flowers? Who?
flow.kid: Look at all 10 flowers. Which have opened? Watch for five minutes. Who visits the open flowers?
flow.parent: Many flowers get few visitors on a high balcony. Write that down too. It is part of the result.
flow.context: In this step of the Bag Test you check the bagged and the open flowers on day 3, and watch for visitors.

flow.do: 1. Look inside each bag without opening it. 2. If the petals have dried or fallen, take that bag off, so that a fruit has room to grow. Leave the thread on. 3. Write the date for each bag you remove.
flow.say: Once the petals have dried, the flower can no longer be pollinated. So the bag can come off now. Leave the thread, so that we know which flowers were bagged.
flow.kid: Look inside each bag. Are the petals dry? Then take the bag off. Leave the thread on.
flow.context: In this step of the Bag Test you take the net bags off the flowers whose petals have dried.

flow.do: 1. Look at the base of each of the 10 flowers. 2. For each, write 'swelling', 'no change' or 'fallen off'.
flow.say: Look at the place where each flower was. Is the ovary swelling? Has the whole flower fallen off?
flow.kid: Look where each flower was. Is the base swelling? Did the flower fall off? Write it down.
flow.context: In this step of the Bag Test you look at the ovary of each flower on day 10.

flow.do: 1. Count the fruits in the bagged group and in the open group. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Then read the note below together. 4. Your child writes a claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
flow.say: Count the fruits in each group. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Count the fruits in each group. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: If the bagged flowers made fruit, where did their pollen come from?
good: From the same flower.
The flower pollinated itself inside the bag.

ask.q: With only 5 flowers in each group, how sure can you be?
good: Not very sure. One fruit more or less could be chance.
I would need more flowers to be sure.

flow.parent: Chilli, tomato, brinjal, bhindi and beans can pollinate themselves. So the bagged flowers often make fruit too, sometimes a little fewer. On a pumpkin, gourd or cucumber vine, bagged female flowers make no fruit. Their pollen must come from a male flower. Either result answers the question. In hot weather many flowers fall off in both groups. Then write that the test could not tell, and try again in a cooler month.
flow.think: Darwin covered 100 heads of red clover, and they made no seeds. What would you say about clover?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Bag Test. You count the fruits from the bagged flowers and the open flowers, and say what the plant needs.

challenges.title: The Pollen Catcher: build a stigma that catches more of the pollen rain
challenges.context: This is a building challenge that follows the Pollen Rain Test. In that test you dropped 100 moong seeds over a small katori, and counted how few landed in it. Now you build a paper catcher on the katori, to catch more of the same rain.
challenges.problem: Use one sheet of paper to build a catcher that stands on the katori. It should catch as many falling moong seeds as possible.
constraints: Use only one sheet of paper from a school notebook, about 20 by 30 centimetres, and 30 centimetres of sticky tape.
The catcher must stand on the katori without being held. The katori stays 30 centimetres from the coin, as in the Pollen Rain Test.
Count every seed that ends in the katori or stays on the catcher. Drop 100 seeds with eyes shut, three times, and add up the three runs.
materials: one sheet of paper from a school notebook
the katori, the bedsheet and the 100 moong seeds from the Pollen Rain Test
general: Roll the paper into a wide cone, like a funnel, with the point in the katori.
Make a flat tray with a folded rim, and rest the tray on the katori.
Cut the paper into a large circle and bend the edge up.
creative: Cut the paper into long strips and spread them out like feathers. Put tape on them, sticky side up, so that seeds stay on.
Make two or three small funnels that lean out in different directions, all leading into the katori.
Make a tall catcher that reaches up towards the tumbler, so the rain has less room to spread.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own catcher and predict how many seeds out of 300 it will catch. Test it. How many times as many seeds did it catch as the bare katori? What feature of a grass stigma or a maize silk does your design share?

setup.art: A small steel katori on a bedsheet beside one sheet of paper, a roll of tape and scissors.
setup.caption: 1. Start with the katori, one sheet of paper and some tape.

setup.art: A paper cone standing with its point in a katori, and a second design with paper strips spread out like feathers.
setup.caption: 2. Build a catcher that stands on the katori by itself.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut shaking moong seeds out of a tumbler over the paper catcher.
setup.caption: 3. Drop 100 seeds, three times. Count the seeds that were caught.

flow.do: 1. Look up the katori's total from the Pollen Rain Test, or do three runs now. 2. Ask your child which features would help a catcher. 3. Your child draws a design and writes a prediction.
flow.say: In the Pollen Rain Test, the bare katori caught only a few seeds out of 300. What would help it catch more? Draw your design. How many seeds will it catch?
flow.kid: The bare katori caught only a few seeds. What would help it catch more? Draw your design. Guess how many seeds it will catch.

ask.q: What could a catcher change: its width, its height or its stickiness? Which matters most, and why?
good: Width, because a wider catcher covers more floor.
Stickiness, so that seeds do not bounce off.
Height, to be closer to where the seeds start.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Pollen Catcher challenge. You plan a paper catcher that will catch more falling seeds than the bare katori did.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds the catcher from one sheet of paper and the tape. 2. Check that it stands on the katori without being held. 3. Do one trial run and let your child change the design once.
flow.say: Build your catcher. It must stand by itself. Try one run, and then you may change one thing.
flow.kid: Build your catcher. Make sure it stands by itself. Try one run. Then change one thing.
flow.parent: A wide cone works well but tips over easily. A few strips of tape from the cone to the katori hold it steady.
flow.context: In this step of the Pollen Catcher challenge you build the catcher and try it once.

flow.do: 1. Do three runs of 100 seeds, with eyes shut. 2. Add up the seeds in the katori and on the catcher. 3. Divide by the bare katori's total. 4. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Do your three runs and add them up. How many times as many seeds did your catcher catch as the bare katori? Which part of your design helped most?
flow.kid: Do three runs. Add up the seeds you caught. Compare with the bare katori. Which part of your design helped most?

ask.q: A grass stigma is feathery and a maize silk is long and hairy. How are they like your catcher?
good: They spread out to cover more space.
They are sticky or hairy, so pollen stays on.

check.q: Why are the stigmas of wind-pollinated flowers long and feathery?
options: To cover more space in the moving air
check.why: Wind-blown pollen lands by chance, so a stigma that reaches through more air catches more grains. Wind flowers do not need to be seen by bees, and they make no nectar.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Pollen Catcher challenge. You test your catcher three times and compare it with the bare katori.

challenges.title: Keep Out Your Own Pollen: design a flower that cannot pollinate itself
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. A flower with stamens and carpels close together can easily pollinate itself. You design a flower, or a plant, in which pollen from the same plant does not reach the stigma. Then you compare your design with five real plants.
challenges.problem: Design a flower or a plant whose own pollen does not land on the plant's own stigmas. The plant must still give pollen to other plants and receive pollen from them.
constraints: The plant must still make pollen and must still have ovules, somewhere.
A visitor or the wind must still be able to take the pollen away, and to bring pollen in.
You may change where the parts are, when they are ripe, or which flowers have which parts. You may not add a lid or a wall that people would have to open.
materials: the table of five real plants in step 2
general: Put the stigma high above the anthers, so that falling pollen cannot reach the stigma.
Make some flowers with only stamens and other flowers with only carpels.
Let the anthers ripen first, and the stigma open only after the pollen has gone.
creative: Put the male flowers and the female flowers on separate plants.
Give the stigma a way to recognise pollen from the same plant and stop that pollen growing a tube.
Make a flower that pollinates itself only on the last day, if no visitor has come.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your own design and label how it keeps out its own pollen. Then say what happens to your plant if no visitor comes and no wind blows. Is the risk worth it?

setup.art: A simple flower drawn with anthers right beside the stigma, and an arrow showing pollen falling from an anther onto the stigma of the same flower.
