flow.do: 1. Draw a simple flower with anthers beside the stigma, and show pollen falling onto the stigma. 2. Ask why a plant might do better with pollen from another plant. 3. Your child draws a design that keeps the plant's own pollen out.
flow.say: This flower's pollen falls on the same flower's stigma. Seeds from two different parents differ more from each other. How could a plant keep out pollen from the same plant? Draw your idea.
flow.kid: This flower's pollen falls on the same flower's stigma. How could a plant keep that pollen out? Draw your idea.

ask.q: Why might seeds with two different parents do better than seeds with one?
good: The young plants differ more from each other.
If a disease comes, some of them may live through it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Keep Out Your Own Pollen challenge. You design a flower that does not pollinate itself.

flow.do: 1. Read these five real plants to your child. Hibiscus: the stigmas stand beyond the anthers. Pumpkin: male flowers and female flowers on one vine. Papaya: male trees and female trees. Custard apple: the stigmas are ready first, and the pollen is shed later. Cabbage: the stigma stops pollen from the same plant. 2. Your child says which real plant is most like their design.
flow.say: Here are five real plants and how each keeps out pollen from the same plant. Which one is most like your design? Which idea did you not think of?
flow.kid: Listen to five real plants. Which one is most like your design? Which idea is new to you?
flow.parent: There are three kinds of answer: keep the parts apart in space, keep them apart in time, or let the stigma recognise the pollen. Most children think of space first.
flow.context: In this step of the Keep Out Your Own Pollen challenge you compare your design with five real plants.

flow.do: 1. Ask what happens to each design if no visitor comes. 2. Tell your child that pea and groundnut flowers pollinate themselves. 3. Your child improves the design, or defends it, and answers the check question.
flow.say: Now the hard part. A female papaya tree stands alone, and no pollen comes. What happens? A pea flower pollinates itself and always sets seed. Which plant takes the bigger risk? Which gets the bigger gain?
flow.kid: A female papaya tree stands alone. No pollen comes. What happens? A pea flower pollinates itself. Which plant takes the bigger risk?

ask.q: When is self-pollination the better way for a plant?
good: When visitors are rare.
When a plant grows alone, far from others of the same kind.

check.q: A pumpkin vine has male flowers and female flowers. What must happen for a pumpkin to grow?
options: Pollen must be carried to a female flower
The male flower must grow into a fruit
The petals must fall off first
check.why: The female flower has the ovary and no pollen. A visitor must carry pollen from a male flower to the stigma of a female flower. A male flower has no ovary, so it can never grow into a fruit.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Keep Out Your Own Pollen challenge. You weigh the risk of needing a visitor against the gain of having two parents.

items.p: Put the four rings of a flower in order, from the outside in.
items.why: The sepals are outside and covered the bud. Then come the petals, then the stamens, and the carpels are in the middle. A strong answer says what each ring does.

items.p: Match each part of a flower to its job.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part has one main job. A strong answer can say why the ovary and the ovule are different: the ovary is the chamber, and the ovules are the grains inside.
pairs: covers the bud before the flower opens
holds the ovules and grows into the fruit
holds an egg cell and can grow into a seed

items.p: Which two parts make up a stamen?
items.why: A stamen is a filament, which is the stalk, with an anther on top. The stigma and style belong to the carpel. Choosing them means the male part and the female part are mixed up.

items.p: The stigma, the style and the ovary together make one ____.
items.why: A carpel is the female part of a flower. The stigma catches pollen, the style joins the stigma to the ovary, and the ovary holds the ovules.

items.p: True or false: pollination and fertilisation are two names for the same event.
items.why: False. Pollination carries pollen to the stigma. Fertilisation comes later, when a male cell joins an egg cell inside an ovule. A strong answer says where each one happens.

items.p: Draw a flower cut in half. Label: sepal, petal, anther, filament, stigma, style, ovary, ovule.
a: Sepal: outer ring, at the base
Anther: the head of a stamen
Filament: the stalk of a stamen
Stigma: the top of the carpel
Style: the stalk of the carpel
Ovary: the swollen base of the carpel
Ovule: a small grain inside the ovary
items.why: A strong drawing shows the stamens around the carpel. It puts the ovules inside the ovary, not on the petals or in the anthers.
items.art: A blank outline of a flower cut in half from top to bottom, with eight empty label lines.

items.p: What is pollination?
opts: Pollen carried from an anther to a stigma
A male cell joining an egg cell
items.why: Pollination is the journey of pollen from an anther to a stigma of the same kind of plant. A male cell joining an egg cell is fertilisation, which comes afterwards.

items.p: Sort these features: do they belong to a wind flower or an animal-visited flower?
items.a: see items
items.why: Animal-visited flowers spend food on being found and on paying the visitor. Wind flowers spend food on extra pollen and on stigmas that reach into the air. A strong answer gives the reason for one feature in each group.

items.p: A pollen grain is on a stigma. Explain how a male cell gets from there to an ovule.
items.a: The pollen grain grows a thin pollen tube. The tube grows down through the style and into the ovary, and enters one ovule. A male cell travels down the tube and joins the egg cell.
items.why: A strong answer names the pollen tube and says that the tube grows through the style to one ovule. It ends with the male cell joining the egg cell.

items.p: Three of these are parts of a carpel. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The stigma, style and ovary make up a carpel. The anther is part of a stamen, the male part.

items.p: True or false: the ovary of a flower grows into the fruit.
items.why: True. After fertilisation the ovary grows into the fruit, and the ovules inside grow into the seeds. A strong answer gives an example, such as a bhindi or a pea pod.

items.p: A pea pod holds 7 full peas and 1 empty place. How many ovules grew into seeds?
items.why: Seven ovules grew into seeds. The pod began with 8 ovules, and 1 stayed tiny. Choosing 8 counts the ovule that never grew.

items.p: Why does a wind-pollinated flower make far more pollen than a bee-pollinated flower?
items.a: Wind-blown pollen lands by chance, and most of it never reaches a stigma. A bee carries pollen straight from flower to flower. So a wind flower must make a huge amount for a few grains to arrive.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence, such as the Pollen Rain Test, where only a few seeds out of 300 landed in the small katori.

items.p: Pollination with pollen from a different plant of the same kind is called ____-pollination.
items.why: In cross-pollination the pollen comes from another plant, so the seed has two different parents. In self-pollination the pollen comes from the same plant.

items.p: Which of these is a fruit to a botanist?
items.why: A bhindi grew from the ovary of a flower and holds seeds, so it is a fruit. A potato is a stem, a carrot is a root, and cabbage is leaves.

items.p: Draw an open pea pod with 5 seeds and 2 empty places. Label one of each, and the sepals.
items.a: The pod is drawn open, with 5 full seeds and 2 tiny grains on short stalks along the seam. The sepals are the green cap at the stalk end.
items.why: A strong drawing shows every seed and every empty place on a stalk, because each began as an ovule.
items.art: A blank outline of an open pea pod with a stalk at one end and a point at the other.

items.p: An ovary holds 10 ovules. Pollen tubes reach 6 of them. How many seeds can form?
items.why: One pollen tube fertilises one ovule, so 6 tubes can start 6 seeds. The other 4 ovules stay as empty places. Choosing 10 means thinking that some pollen is enough for all.

items.p: A maize cob is bare at the tip and full below. Give a reason, using what a silk is.
items.a: Each silk is the style of one ovule, and a kernel grows only if that silk catches a pollen grain. The silks from the tip come out last. By then little pollen may be left, so those ovules are not fertilised.
items.why: A strong answer says one silk for one kernel, and links the bare tip to silks that caught no pollen.

items.p: Sort each case: is it self-pollination or cross-pollination?
items.a: see items
items.why: Self-pollination uses pollen from the same plant, even from another flower on that plant. Cross-pollination uses pollen from a different plant. A strong answer explains the case of two flowers on one plant.
items: pollen lands on the stigma of the same flower
pollen goes to another flower on the same plant
pollen comes from a plant across the field
a pea bud is pollinated before the bud opens
a female papaya tree gets pollen from a male tree
a bee carries pollen from one mango tree to another

items.p: A pollen grain on a stigma grows a pollen ____ down through the style.
items.why: The pollen tube is thinner than a hair. It carries the male cells from the pollen grain down to an ovule.

items.p: A flower is red, with a lot of thin nectar and almost no scent. Who most likely pollinates it?
items.why: Birds see red well, drink a lot of nectar and find flowers mostly by sight. Moths are guided by scent at night, and wind flowers have no nectar at all.

items.p: Put these events in order, from pollen to fruit.
a: A pollen tube grows down the style
A male cell joins the egg cell
The ovule grows into a seed and the ovary into a fruit
items.why: Pollination comes first, then the tube, then fertilisation, and only then the seed and the fruit. A strong answer says which step is pollination and which is fertilisation.
items: A male cell joins the egg cell
The ovule grows into a seed and the ovary into a fruit
A pollen tube grows down the style

items.p: True or false: a marigold is a single flower with many petals.
items.why: False. A marigold is a head of many small flowers. Each piece has an ovary and a stigma of its own, and a petal has neither.

items.p: What were the dry brown threads at the tip of a maize cob, when the cob was young?
items.why: Each thread is a silk, which is the style of one ovule. Pollen lands on the silk, and a pollen tube grows down it to the ovule.

items.p: A bowl is 3 times as wide as a katori. Why does it catch about 9 times as many seeds?
items.a: A bowl 3 times as wide is also 3 times as long. So it covers 3 × 3 = 9 times as much floor. Seeds fall over the whole floor, so the bowl catches about 9 times as many.
items.why: A strong answer says that catching depends on the area covered, and shows 3 × 3 = 9.

items.p: Three of these plants are pollinated by wind. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Paddy, maize and doob grass have small dull flowers with hanging anthers, and the wind carries their pollen. Pumpkin flowers are large and yellow, with nectar, and bees pollinate them.

items.p: Match each part of a fruit to the part of the flower that it grew from.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A fruit keeps signs of the flower. A strong answer can point to these signs on a real fruit in the kitchen.
pairs: The green cap on a brinjal
The dry point at the tip of a pea pod
The green wall of a pea pod

items.p: A banana has tiny dark specks in the middle, and no seeds. What are the specks?
items.why: The bananas we eat grow without fertilisation. The ovules stay tiny and turn dark. Wild bananas, which are fertilised, are full of hard seeds.

items.p: A papaya tree flowers every year but never gives fruit. Give two possible reasons.
items.a: The tree may be a male tree, with flowers that have stamens and no ovary. Or the tree may be female, with no male tree near enough for pollen to arrive.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that some plants keep male flowers and female flowers on separate plants.

items.p: True or false: one pollen grain can fertilise all the ovules in an ovary.
items.why: False. One pollen grain grows one tube, and one tube fertilises one ovule. An ovary with 8 ovules needs at least 8 pollen grains to fill every place.

items.p: A farmer's pumpkin vines make few pumpkins, because few bees come to the field. Two farmers suggest what to do.
items.a: A strong answer sees the trade-off. Hand pollination is sure and quick to start, but it takes time every morning and cannot cover a large field. Bringing back bees takes a season or more, but then the bees pollinate every flower, for every crop.
items.why: There is no single right answer. The best choice depends on the size of the field and how long the farmer can wait.

views.who: A farmer who pollinates by hand
views.says: Each morning I pick a male flower and dab the pollen on the female flowers. It is sure, and it costs only my time.

views.who: A farmer who plants for bees
views.says: I stop spraying and grow a strip of flowers beside the field. The bees come back and visit thousands of flowers that I could never reach.

items.ask: Which would you choose for ten vines? Which for a whole field? Give a reason for each, and one weakness of your choice.

items.p: Draw a wind-pollinated flower and an insect-pollinated flower side by side. Label three differences.
items.a: The wind flower has no bright petals, anthers hanging out on long filaments, and feathery stigmas. The insect flower has bright petals, nectar, and a sticky stigma inside the flower.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a reason for each difference: what helps pollen leave on the wind, and what brings a visitor.
items.art: Two blank boxes side by side, headed Wind and Insect.

items.p: A pea pod holds five peas. Three people describe the same pod.
items.a: A strong answer sees that each view is true of a part. The pod is one ovary of the mother plant. Each pea began at a separate fertilisation and can grow into a separate plant. The cook's meaning is about use.
items.why: The question has no single winner. It shows that 'one' depends on what you are counting.

views.says: This is one vegetable. I buy pods by weight, and one pod goes into the pan as one thing.
This is one fruit. One ovary of one flower grew into this pod, and the mother plant built the whole pod.

views.who: A child who counted the seeds
views.says: This is five young plants in a shared case. Each began with a different pollen grain, and each can grow alone.

items.ask: Whose way of counting do you agree with most? Give your evidence. Then say what one of the others sees that you do not.

items.p: A stigma lets some pollen grains grow tubes and stops others. Two botanists disagree about what to call this.
items.a: A strong answer says what both agree on: the stigma tells kinds of pollen apart and treats them differently. It then says what the word 'choose' adds. It suggests evidence, such as testing whether one stigma acts differently at different times.
items.why: This is a real argument. It turns on what we mean by choosing, and on what evidence could show it.

views.says: The plant senses whose pollen has arrived and decides which grains may grow. That is choosing, done without a brain.
Proteins on the pollen fit the stigma or they do not, as a key fits a lock. That is chemistry, and we should not call it choosing.

items.ask: Which botanist do you agree with? Give one reason. What evidence would make you change your mind?

items.p: A scientist claims the young plant comes ready-made inside the pollen tube. What would you look for to test this?
items.a: Look inside ovules before any pollen tube has arrived. If an egg cell is already there, the tube did not bring the young plant. Then watch whether the young plant grows from that egg cell.
items.why: A strong answer looks at the ovule before the tube arrives, and says what each result would mean.

items.p: Covered clover heads made no seeds. Open heads made 2,700. What does this show, and not show?
items.a: Darwin covered 100 heads of red clover and left 100 open. The result shows that red clover needs visitors to carry pollen, because the covered flowers made no seeds. It does not show that every plant needs visitors. Pea flowers pollinate themselves and would set seed under a cover.
items.why: A strong answer keeps the conclusion to the plant that was tested, and names a plant that would behave differently.

items.p: Pollen from a hibiscus lands on the stigma of a pumpkin flower. What most likely happens?
opts: A hibiscus fruit grows on the vine
items.why: Pollen must be of the same kind of plant. Pollen of another kind usually grows no tube, or the tube stops in the style. Without fertilisation, no seeds form.

items.p: A lopsided apple has seeds only on the round side. Explain why the apple grew like this.
items.a: The ovules on the flat side were not fertilised, so no seeds grew there. Young seeds send a signal that makes the fruit around them grow. With no seeds on one side, that side grew less.
items.why: A strong answer links the missing seeds to missing fertilisation, and then links seeds to the growth of the fruit.

items.p: Which finding best supports the idea that each ovule is fertilised separately?
opts: A pod with seeds beside empty places
All the pods on a plant are green
Every flower on a plant has petals
items.why: If one event fertilised a whole ovary, a pod would be all full or all empty. Seeds beside empty places show that each ovule had a separate chance.

items.p: True or false: the white part of a rice grain grew from a second joining of cells.
items.why: True. A pollen tube carries two male cells. One joins the egg cell and becomes the embryo. The other joins another cell, and that joining grows into the food store of the grain.

items.p: In a pine, pollen lands right beside an open ovule. What is different in a flowering plant?
opts: The ovules are sealed inside an ovary
items.why: In a flowering plant the ovules are shut inside the carpel. Pollen lands on the stigma outside, and must grow a tube through the style to reach an ovule.

items.p: Match each plant to the way that plant keeps out pollen from the same plant.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Plants keep the male and female parts apart in space or in time, or the stigma recognises the pollen. A strong answer says which of the three each one is.
pairs: the stigmas stand beyond the anthers
male flowers and female flowers on one vine
the stigmas are ready before the pollen is shed
the stigma stops pollen from the same plant

items.p: Sort these: did each one grow from one flower, or from many flowers?
items.a: see items
items.why: A mango, a pea pod and a tomato each grew from the ovary of one flower. A pineapple and a jackfruit each grew from a whole bunch of flowers joined together. A sunflower head holds the fruits of many small flowers.
items: a sunflower head full of seeds

items.p: Plan a fair test: does a tomato flower need an insect to make fruit? What would you cover and count?
items.a: Cover some closed buds with net bags, so that no insect can reach them. Leave the same number of buds open on the same plant. Count how many flowers in each group grow into fruits. Use many buds, because a few could differ by chance.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing, covers the buds before they open, and counts fruits in both groups.

items.p: Draw a pollen tube arriving at an ovule. Label the two male cells, the egg cell and what each becomes.
items.a: The tube tip is drawn inside the ovule, with two male cells. One male cell joins the egg cell, and this becomes the embryo. The other joins another cell in the ovule, and this becomes the food store of the seed.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two separate joinings, and labels what grows from each.
items.art: A blank outline of an ovule drawn large, with a small opening at one end.

items.p: A stigma receives 200 pollen grains, and the ovary holds 20 ovules. What is the largest number of seeds?
items.why: Each seed needs one ovule and one pollen tube. There are only 20 ovules, so at most 20 seeds. The other pollen grains find no ovule left.

items.p: Seeds are picked off one side of a young strawberry, and that side stops growing. What does this suggest?
items.a: It suggests that the young seeds send a signal that makes the fruit around them grow. Where the seeds are removed, the signal stops and so does the growth.
items.why: A strong answer says that the seeds cause the growth of the fruit. It notes that the other side, with its seeds, kept growing.

items.p: True or false: all the seeds in one fruit must have the same father plant.
items.why: False. Each ovule is fertilised by a separate pollen grain. If pollen from several plants lands on one stigma, the seeds in one fruit can have different fathers.

quiz.p: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
quiz.why: The anther is the head of a stamen, and pollen forms inside it. The stigma catches pollen but does not make it.

quiz.p: Which three parts make up a carpel?
quiz.why: A carpel has a stigma on top, a style in the middle and an ovary at the base. The anther and filament make up a stamen.

quiz.p: What is the main job of the sepals?
quiz.why: The sepals wrap the bud before the flower opens. Pollen is made by the anthers and caught by the stigma, and the ovary holds the ovules.

quiz.p: A bee carries pollen from one mango tree to another mango tree. What is this called?
quiz.why: The pollen comes from a different plant of the same kind, so this is cross-pollination. Fertilisation happens later, inside the ovule.

quiz.p: A flower has no petals, no scent, hanging anthers and feathery stigmas. How is it pollinated?
quiz.why: These are the features of a wind flower. It has nothing to bring a visitor, and its anthers and stigmas reach out into the moving air.

quiz.p: Pollen has landed on a stigma. What must happen before a seed can begin?
opts: A male cell reaches an egg cell
quiz.why: The pollen grain grows a tube down to an ovule, and a male cell joins the egg cell. That joining is fertilisation. Choosing another answer treats pollination as the end of the story.
The egg cell is inside the ovule, in the ovary. The pollen lands on the stigma, but the cells join only when the tube reaches the ovule.

quiz.p: After fertilisation, what does each ovule grow into?
quiz.why: Each fertilised ovule grows into a seed. The ovary around the ovules grows into the fruit. Choosing the fruit mixes up the ovule and the ovary.

quiz.p: The green star on top of a tomato grew from which part of the flower?
quiz.why: The sepals often stay on the fruit after the petals and stamens have fallen. The tomato below them grew from the ovary.

quiz.p: A bean ovary holds 9 ovules. Pollen tubes reach 6 of them. What will the ripe pod hold?
quiz.why: Each ovule needs their own pollen tube. Six were fertilised and grew into seeds. The other three stayed tiny, as empty places.

quiz.p: A maize cob has a bare patch with no kernels. What is the most likely reason?
opts: The silks there caught no pollen
The plant had too much sun
The cob had no ovules there
quiz.why: Each kernel has one silk, and grows only if that silk catches a pollen grain. The bare patch had ovules and silks, but no pollen reached them.

quiz.p: Why did the Empty Places Test use 20 pods, and not 1?
opts: Pods must be counted in twenties
quiz.why: Pods differ from each other. One pod might be full, or half empty, by chance. Counting 20 shows what usually happens.

applications: Farmers who grow date palms, custard apples and vanilla carry pollen to the flowers by hand, to be sure of fruit.
Fruit growers keep beehives in apple, mustard and sunflower fields at flowering time, so that more flowers are pollinated.
Farmers and gardeners sow maize in blocks, not in single lines. Then wind-blown pollen falls on the silks of neighbouring plants.
Plant breeders make a new variety by putting the pollen of one chosen parent on the stigma of another. Then they cover the flower.
Seed companies grow two parent lines of maize side by side and remove the tassels from one. Then every seed has the other line as father.
Weather offices in some cities count the pollen in the air, to warn people whose noses and eyes react to pollen.
Scientists read pollen grains in old mud to learn which plants grew in a place thousands of years ago.
Growers of seedless watermelons and bananas use plants whose fruits grow without ripe seeds inside.

open_questions.q: How does a mother plant decide which young seeds to feed?
open_questions.why_open: Plants drop many young fruits and stop feeding some seeds. Scientists know some of the signals, but they cannot yet predict which seed a plant will keep.

open_questions.q: How do the pollen and the stigma of most plants recognise each other?
open_questions.why_open: The proteins that do this are known in a few plant families, such as the cabbage family. For most kinds of plants nobody has found them yet.

open_questions.q: What did the first flower look like, and who pollinated it?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest fossil flowers are about 130 million years old, and fossils of flowers are rare. Scientists have drawn the first flower from the family tree of living plants, but no fossil of that flower has been found.

open_questions.q: Can a flower sense that a visitor is near?
open_questions.why_open: In 2019, scientists reported that evening primrose flowers made sweeter nectar within minutes of the sound of a flying bee. Other scientists want to see the test repeated, and nobody knows how many flowers can do this.

open_questions.q: Can food crops be made to form seeds without fertilisation?
open_questions.why_open: A few wild plants make seeds that are copies of the mother. In 2019, scientists made rice plants do this in a laboratory. Nobody knows yet whether it will work well in farmers' fields.

maths.problem: In one Empty Places Test, 20 pods held 160 ovules. 132 of the ovules became seeds. What percent of the ovules became seeds?
maths.explain: 132 ÷ 160 = 0.825. As a percent that is 82.5, which is about 83 percent. So about 5 ovules in every 6 became seeds.
maths.context: In the Empty Places Test, you count the full seeds and the tiny ovules that never grew, in 20 pods.
maths.why_maths: A percent lets you compare your pods with someone else's, even if they counted a different number of pods.

maths.problem: In the Pollen Rain Test, a katori 7 centimetres wide caught 5 seeds. A bowl is 21 centimetres wide. If catching depends on the area covered, about how many seeds would the bowl catch?
maths.explain: 21 ÷ 7 = 3, so the bowl is 3 times as wide. Area grows in both directions, so the bowl covers 3 × 3 = 9 times the area. 5 × 9 = 45 seeds.
maths.context: In the Pollen Rain Test, you drop moong seeds over a small katori and a wide bowl. You count how many land in each.
maths.why_maths: Thinking about area explains why a catcher three times as wide catches about nine times as much.

maths.problem: A maize cob has 16 rows with 32 places in each row. 28 of the places are bare. How many kernels grew? What fraction of the places is bare, in its simplest form?
maths.answer: 484 kernels. 7 out of 128 places are bare.
maths.explain: 16 × 32 = 512 places. 512 − 28 = 484 kernels. 28 out of 512 is the same as 7 out of 128, after dividing both by 4.
maths.context: In One Silk, One Kernel, you count the rows on a maize cob and the kernels in a row. You also look for bare places.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying rows by places is much faster than counting 500 kernels one at a time.

maths.problem: A young maize cob has 500 silks. Only 1 pollen grain in every 100 that fall near the cob lands on a silk. How many grains must fall near the cob for every silk to get one?
maths.explain: Each silk needs 1 grain, so 500 grains must land. Only 1 in 100 lands, so 500 × 100 = 50,000 grains must fall.
maths.context: In the Pollen Rain Test, most of the seeds you dropped missed the small katori. Wind-blown pollen misses most stigmas in the same way.
maths.why_maths: The ratio turns 'most pollen is wasted' into a number, and shows why one maize tassel sheds millions of grains.

maths.problem: A maize pollen grain is 0.1 millimetres wide. The pollen tube grows down a silk 20 centimetres long. How many times the grain's own width is that?
maths.explain: 20 centimetres is 200 millimetres. 200 ÷ 0.1 = 2,000. If the grain were a marble 1 centimetre wide, the tube would be 20 metres long.
maths.context: In the Hidden Journey, you draw the pollen tube that grows from a pollen grain down to an ovule.
maths.why_maths: Scaling the grain up to the size of a marble makes a length you cannot see into one you can pace out.

maths.problem: Darwin counted seeds on clover heads that bees could visit. 100 heads of red clover made 2,700 seeds. 20 heads of white clover made 2,290 seeds. Which clover made more seeds on each head, and about how many times as many?
maths.answer: White clover, about 4 times as many.
maths.explain: Red clover: 2,700 ÷ 100 = 27 seeds on a head. White clover: 2,290 ÷ 20 = 114.5 seeds on a head. 114.5 ÷ 27 is a little more than 4.
maths.context: In the Bag Test, you compare flowers that visitors can reach with flowers under a net. Darwin did the same with clover, and the covered heads made no seeds.
maths.why_maths: The totals cannot be compared directly, because Darwin counted 100 heads of one clover and 20 of the other. Dividing gives seeds for one head.

maths.problem: A pod has 8 ovules. Suppose each ovule has a 3 in 4 chance of becoming a seed. How many seeds would you expect in the pod? Will every such pod hold exactly that many?
maths.answer: 6 seeds on average. No, single pods will differ.
maths.explain: 3 quarters of 8 is 6. That is the average over many pods. One pod may hold 4 and another 8, because chance decides each ovule separately.
maths.context: In the Empty Places Test, your 20 pods did not all have the same number of empty places.
maths.why_maths: Chance explains why pods from the same plant differ, and why you need many pods to find the usual share.

warmup.q: Name the four rings of a flower, from the outside in.
Which part of a flower makes pollen?
warmup.a: The anther, which is the head of a stamen.

warmup.q: What are the three parts of a carpel?
warmup.a: The stigma on top, the style in the middle and the ovary at the base.

warmup.q: What is the difference between pollination and fertilisation?
warmup.a: Pollination carries pollen to a stigma. Fertilisation joins a male cell and an egg cell inside an ovule.

warmup.q: How does a male cell get from the stigma to an ovule?
warmup.a: The pollen grain grows a pollen tube down through the style.

warmup.q: Which part of the flower becomes the fruit, and which becomes a seed?
warmup.a: The ovary becomes the fruit. Each fertilised ovule becomes a seed.

warmup.q: Name two features of a wind-pollinated flower.
warmup.a: Any two of: no bright petals, no scent, no nectar, hanging anthers, feathery stigmas, a lot of light pollen.

warmup.q: Why can a pod have an empty place?
warmup.a: Each ovule needs their own pollen tube. An ovule that was not fertilised, or that stopped growing, stays tiny.

quiz: The anther makes pollen.
The anther is the head of a stamen, and pollen forms inside it.
Pollination and fertilisation are the same event.
Pollination carries pollen to the stigma. Fertilisation joins two cells inside the ovule.
The ovary of a flower grows into the fruit.
The ovules inside the ovary grow into the seeds.
One pollen grain can fertilise every ovule in a flower.
One pollen grain grows one tube, and one tube fertilises one ovule.
A paddy flower has bright petals to bring bees.
Paddy is pollinated by wind. The flower has no petals, no scent and no nectar.
Each silk on a maize cob leads to one kernel.
A silk is the style of one ovule.
A marigold is a head of many small flowers.
Each piece has an ovary and a stigma of its own.
A tomato is a fruit to a botanist.
A tomato grew from the ovary of a flower and holds seeds.
A pollen tube grows up from the ovule to the stigma.
The tube grows down, from the pollen grain on the stigma to the ovule.
Pea flowers usually pollinate themselves.
A pea flower sheds pollen on its own stigma inside the closed bud.
odd: The first three are parts of a carpel. The anther is part of a stamen.
Paddy, maize and grass are pollinated by wind. Animals pollinate the hibiscus.
The first three are fruits that grew from an ovary. A potato is a stem.
Bees, sunbirds and moths carry pollen between flowers. Earthworms live in the soil.
Sepals, petals and stamens are parts of a flower. A root is not.

science: Amici G. B. (1824). Osservazioni microscopiche sopra varie piante. Atti della Societa Italiana delle Scienze 19. The first report of a pollen tube, seen on purslane in 1823. Amici followed tubes into the ovule by 1830, and reported on orchids at the meeting of Italian scientists in Genoa in 1846.

Schleiden M. J. (1837). Einige Blicke auf die Entwicklungsgeschichte des vegetabilischen Organismus bei den Phanerogamen. Archiv fur Naturgeschichte 3. The claim that the tip of the pollen tube becomes the embryo, later shown to be wrong.

Nawaschin S. (1898). Resultate einer Revision der Befruchtungsvorgange bei Lilium martagon und Fritillaria tenella. Bulletin de l'Academie Imperiale des Sciences de St. Petersbourg 9. The discovery that a pollen tube brings two male cells, and that both join cells in the ovule.

Darwin C. (1859). On the Origin of Species, chapter 3. 100 heads of red clover visited by bees made 2,700 seeds and 100 protected heads made none. 20 heads of white clover made 2,290 seeds and 20 protected heads made none.

Nitsch J. P. (1950). Growth and morphogenesis of the strawberry as related to auxin. American Journal of Botany 37: 211-215. Removing the small fruits (achenes) from a young strawberry stops the growth of the flesh beneath them.

Higashiyama T. et al. (2001). Pollen tube attraction by the synergid cell. Science 293: 1480-1483. Okuda S. et al. (2009). Defensin-like polypeptide LUREs are pollen tube attractants secreted from synergid cells. Nature 458: 357-361.
Ollerton J., Winfree R., Tarrant S. (2011). How many flowering plants are pollinated by animals? Oikos 120: 321-326. The source of 'nearly 9 out of 10 kinds'.

Veits M. et al. (2019). Flowers respond to pollinator sound within minutes by increasing nectar sugar concentration. Ecology Letters 22: 1483-1492. The evening primrose finding, which still needs to be repeated by others.

Khanday I. et al. (2019). A male-expressed rice embryogenic trigger redirected for asexual propagation through seeds. Nature 565: 91-95. Rice plants that form seeds without fertilisation, in a laboratory.

General botany, as in standard textbooks: one silk for each maize ovule; self-incompatibility in the cabbage family; the stigmas of custard apple ripening before the anthers; seedless bananas forming without fertilisation; the oldest fossil flowers at about 125 to 130 million years.

playtest: Read through step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would use it. The experiments were reasoned through carefully but have not been tried at home. Please treat the expected results as likely and not certain. Take a Flower Apart needs one single hibiscus with five petals. Double hibiscus flowers with many petals do not show the rings clearly. The ovules in the cut ovary are very small, and a phone camera on zoom shows them better than the eye. The Empty Places Test needs 20 fresh pods. Green peas in the pod are best, and are sold mostly from November to March. At other times use flat beans, fresh tuvar, double beans or long beans. The tiny ovules that never grew are easy to miss in the first pod. Look at the two ends of the seam with a lens. Pods in a shop are often picked full, so the share of ovules that became seeds may be high. By looking, nobody can tell an ovule that was never fertilised from one that stopped growing soon afterwards. The unit says so. The Pollen Rain Test needs 100 moong seeds, a small katori, a wide bowl and a bedsheet. The katori often catches no seeds at all in a run, which is why the three runs are added up. The seeds roll, so collect them from the sheet before a young child or a pet finds them. The Bag Test needs a plant with at least ten buds and is marked 'if you have a plant in flower'. Chilli, tomato, brinjal, bhindi and beans usually make fruit inside the bag, because they can pollinate themselves. That is a real result. In hot weather many flowers fall off in both groups. One Silk, One Kernel needs a maize cob still in the husk, which is easiest to buy in the rains. The Marigold Count works with any marigold from a garland. The games need paper, a die and moong seeds, and both can be played alone. Facts to treat with care: the numbers of chambers in fruits vary from fruit to fruit, so the child writes what they count. The sizes and speeds given for maize pollen and pollen tubes are rounded. The finding that flowers respond to the sound of a bee comes from one study and has not yet been repeated. Two of the three films were found by search and confirmed by title only, so a parent should watch them first.
